a.title: A Day for Animals
text: October 4 is World Animal Day. It is a day to think about animals and how we treat them.
Animals share our world. Some live in our homes, like cats and dogs. Others live in forests, oceans, and the sky.
On this day, people learn how to care for animals. They talk about pets, farm animals, and wild animals in danger.
Many animals need our help. Some lose their homes when forests are cut down. Some need a kind family to adopt them.
You can help too. Be gentle with pets. Give them food, water, and love. Never leave an animal alone in the cold.
When we are kind to animals, the whole world becomes a better home for everyone.

b.title: Sharing the Planet
text: Every year on 4 October, people mark World Animal Day, a global event that asks a simple question: how well do we treat the creatures we share the planet with?
The date honours Saint Francis of Assisi, a man remembered for his love of animals. Today it is used to raise awareness of animal welfare all over the world.

The concerns are wide. Pets are sometimes abandoned when families no longer want them. Farm animals are often kept in poor conditions. And in the wild, many species are losing their homes as forests are cleared and the climate warms.

There is also good news. Animal shelters find new homes for millions of pets each year, and laws in many countries now protect animals from cruelty. Some once-endangered species have slowly recovered.
Small choices matter. Adopting a pet instead of buying one, supporting local shelters, and simply treating animals with respect all make a difference.
The message of the day is gentle but important: animals cannot speak for themselves, so it is up to people to speak, and act, for them.

c.title: The Creatures We Live Among
text: Each 4 October, World Animal Day invites a reckoning of sorts: an annual pause to ask what humans owe the millions of other species with which they share a crowded planet.

The day traces its spirit to Saint Francis of Assisi, the medieval friar who spoke of animals as brothers and sisters. Yet its modern purpose is less devotional than practical — to focus attention on animal welfare, from the family pet to the vanishing tiger.

The moral landscape is complicated. Few people wish animals harm, and yet human choices — what we eat, what we buy, how we build — shape the fate of countless creatures we will never see. Habitat loss, driven by farming and a warming climate, remains the greatest threat to wild species.

Progress, where it exists, tends to be quiet. Stronger animal-protection laws, the steady work of shelters and sanctuaries, and shifting attitudes toward adoption have all improved millions of individual lives, even as the larger picture stays fragile.

Perhaps that is the day's real lesson: that kindness to animals is not sentimentality but a measure of a society's character, and that a species clever enough to reshape the Earth bears some responsibility for the others living on it.

a.title: Turning Brain Cells On with Light
text: On October 5, 2026, three scientists won the Nobel Prize in Medicine. Their names are Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel.
They found a way to control brain cells with light. This idea is called optogenetics.
The brain has billions of tiny cells. These cells send signals that make us move, think, and feel.
The scientists took a special protein from algae — tiny green plants that live in water. This protein reacts to light.
They put the protein inside brain cells. Now, when light shines on a cell, the cell turns on. When the light stops, the cell turns off.
This tool helps scientists understand the brain. One day, it may even help blind people see again.

b.title: Optogenetics: Switching Neurons On and Off
text: On 5 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel for a powerful technique known as optogenetics.

The brain is made of billions of nerve cells, or neurons, that communicate using tiny electrical signals. For a long time, scientists could watch these signals, but they could not switch a single neuron on or off whenever they wanted.
The breakthrough began with green algae. Hegemann and Nagel discovered that these simple organisms carry light-sensitive proteins called channelrhodopsins, which open when light hits them.
Deisseroth then had a bold idea: place these proteins inside neurons. Shine a blue light, and the neuron fires; take the light away, and it falls silent — all within milliseconds.
This gave researchers a precise 'switch' for the brain. By turning chosen neurons on and off, they can study how brain circuits control movement, memory, and mood.
Optogenetics is also moving toward medicine. In one remarkable case reported in Nature Medicine, light-sensitive proteins helped restore partial vision to a man who had been blind for decades.

c.title: A Light Switch for the Mind
text: When the Nobel Assembly announced the 2026 Prize in Physiology or Medicine on 5 October, it honoured a discovery that has quietly transformed neuroscience: optogenetics, the art of controlling individual neurons with nothing more than a beam of light.

The award was shared equally by Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, and Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel of Germany. Their work answered a question that had frustrated researchers for generations — how to study the living brain not by observing it, but by commanding it.

The key came from an unlikely source: pond-dwelling green algae. Hegemann and Nagel showed that these microbes steer toward light using proteins called channelrhodopsins, molecular gates that spring open the instant light strikes them.

Deisseroth's insight was to borrow these gates and install them in mammalian neurons. A pulse of blue light could now make a chosen neuron fire, while darkness silenced it — with a speed and precision that earlier methods could never match.

The consequences were profound. Because behaviour, emotion and memory all arise from the firing of particular circuits, scientists could finally test cause and effect directly, switching circuits on and off to see exactly what each one does.

The technique is now reaching the clinic. In a landmark trial published in Nature Medicine, optogenetic therapy restored a measure of sight to a patient blinded by an inherited eye disease — a hint of future treatments for blindness, paralysis and disorders of the brain.

a.title: Thank You, Teachers
text: October 5 is World Teachers' Day. It is a day to say thank you to teachers everywhere.
Teachers help us learn to read, write, count, and think. They also teach us how to be kind and work with others.
A good teacher does more than give lessons. They listen, they care, and they help students believe in themselves.
Being a teacher is not easy. They work long hours, plan lessons, and worry about every student.
In many countries, there are not enough teachers. The world needs millions more so that every child can go to school.
On this day, we say two small but powerful words to our teachers: thank you.

b.title: The People Who Shape Us
text: Each year on 5 October, UNESCO leads the world in celebrating World Teachers' Day, a moment to honour the people who quietly shape every other profession.
Teachers do far more than deliver facts. They spark curiosity, build confidence, and are often the first adults outside the family to believe in a child's future.

Yet the job is under strain. Many teachers work long unpaid hours, face crowded classrooms, and earn less than others with similar training. In some places, respect for the profession has slowly faded.
The world also faces a shortage. The United Nations estimates that tens of millions of new teachers are needed so that every child can receive a decent education, especially in poorer regions.
Technology is changing the classroom too. Useful tools, and even AI, can support teaching, but few believe they can replace the patience, warmth, and judgement of a real teacher.
The day's message is simple: a society that wants a better future must value, support, and fairly pay the people it trusts to build it.

c.title: In Praise of the Teacher
text: On 5 October the world observes World Teachers' Day, an occasion easy to sentimentalise and just as easy to overlook. Behind the greeting cards lies a serious claim: that no profession does more to determine a nation's future, and few are asked to do so much with so little.

The work resists measurement. A teacher's influence — a question that sparks a career, a word of belief on a hard day — often surfaces years later, in lives the teacher never sees. What can be measured tells a harder story: rising workloads, stagnant pay, and, in many places, a slow erosion of public respect.

The result is a global shortage. UNESCO warns that the world needs tens of millions more teachers to meet its education goals, a gap widest precisely where schooling is most needed. Recruiting them is one thing; keeping them, when so many leave within a few years, is another.

Into this arrives technology, promising to lighten the load. Well-designed tools can indeed help, but the enthusiasm for automation can obscure a stubborn truth: learning is relational. A screen can deliver information; it cannot notice the quiet child at the back of the room.
That, in the end, is what the day defends — not a job title, but a human relationship on which almost everything else depends.

a.title: A Giant Telescope Made of Ice
text: On October 6, 2026, a scientist named Francis Halzen won the Nobel Prize in Physics.
He helped build IceCube, a huge detector deep in the ice of Antarctica, near the South Pole.
IceCube hunts for tiny particles called neutrinos. They are so small that they fly right through you — and through the whole Earth!
Trillions of neutrinos pass through your body every second, but you never feel them.
Once in a while, a neutrino hits the ice and makes a tiny blue flash of light. Thousands of sensors in the ice can see it.
Some neutrinos come from faraway, powerful events in space. By catching them, scientists can study the universe in a brand-new way.

b.title: IceCube: Hunting Ghost Particles at the South Pole
text: On 6 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Francis Halzen for his leading role in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos from space.

Neutrinos are among the strangest particles in nature. They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything. Trillions stream through your body every second without leaving a trace.
That makes them incredibly hard to catch. To do it, scientists turned a cubic kilometre of clear Antarctic ice into a detector, burying over 5,000 light sensors deep beneath the South Pole.
Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow. The sensors record this light and reveal where the particle came from.
In 2013, IceCube found the first neutrinos born far beyond our solar system, in some of the most violent events in the universe.
Because neutrinos travel in straight lines and pass through almost everything, they carry clues that ordinary light cannot. Halzen's work opened a new field: neutrino astronomy.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Neutrinos have almost no mass and hardly interact with anything.
By turning Antarctic ice into a giant detector, IceCube catches cosmic neutrinos — work that won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.
q.why: 核心：IceCube 把南極冰變成巨型偵測器捕捉宇宙微中子，獲 2026 諾貝爾物理獎。

q.q: Why are neutrinos hard to catch?
opts: They have almost no mass and hardly interact with anything
q.why: 微中子幾乎沒有質量、極少與物質作用，所以很難捕捉。

q.q: How does IceCube detect a neutrino?
opts: By recording the faint blue light made when a neutrino hits the ice
q.why: 微中子撞冰時產生微弱藍光，感應器記錄下來。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “trace” means ___.
opts: a sign or mark left behind
q.why: trace ＝ 留下的痕跡。

q.q: Why do neutrinos carry clues that light cannot?
opts: They travel in straight lines and pass through almost everything
They are much brighter than ordinary light
q.why: 微中子走直線又能穿透幾乎一切，帶來光無法傳遞的訊息。

tr.en: They have almost no mass, carry no electric charge, and hardly ever bump into anything.
tr.zh: 它們幾乎沒有質量、不帶電荷，而且幾乎從不撞上任何東西。

tr.en: Now and then, a neutrino crashes into the ice and creates a faint blue glow.
tr.zh: 偶爾會有一個微中子撞進冰裡，產生微弱的藍光。

tr.en: In 2013, IceCube found the first neutrinos born far beyond our solar system, in some of the most violent events in the universe.
tr.zh: 2013 年，冰立方找到了第一批誕生在太陽系之外遙遠地方的微中子，它們來自宇宙中一些最劇烈的事件。

c.title: Reading the Universe with Neutrinos
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy named Francis Halzen the 2026 Nobel laureate in Physics on 6 October, it recognised a discovery that gave astronomers an entirely new sense: the ability to 'see' the cosmos through neutrinos.
Neutrinos are nature's great escape artists. Nearly massless and electrically neutral, they interact so weakly that most slip through the entire Earth as though it were empty space.

Capturing them demanded an instrument of extraordinary scale. Under Halzen's leadership, the IceCube Observatory transformed a cubic kilometre of pristine Antarctic ice into a detector, threaded with thousands of sensors more than a kilometre below the surface.

On the rare occasion that a neutrino strikes an atom in the ice, it releases a ghostly blue flash. From the pattern of light, scientists can reconstruct the particle's energy and trace its path back across the sky.
In 2013, IceCube detected the first high-energy neutrinos of cosmic origin, later linking some to distant galaxies with supermassive black holes at their hearts.

Unlike light, neutrinos stream unblocked from the universe's most hidden and violent corners. Halzen's achievement founded neutrino astronomy, opening a fresh window onto events no ordinary telescope could ever observe.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How IceCube lets scientists study the universe through neutrinos, earning the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
How IceCube detected the first high-energy neutrinos in 2013
A new kind of telescope lens
q.why: 全文講 IceCube 以微中子研究宇宙，獲 2026 諾貝爾物理獎。

q.q: What did IceCube achieve in 2013?
opts: It melted a kilometre of ice
It detected the first high-energy neutrinos from beyond our solar system
q.why: 2013 年 IceCube 偵測到第一批來自太陽系外的高能微中子。

q.q: Why build the detector inside Antarctic ice?
opts: Clear, pristine ice lets sensors spot the faint flash from a rare neutrino hit
q.why: 純淨透明的冰讓感應器能看見罕見的微弱閃光。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “laureate” means ___.
q.why: laureate ＝ 得獎者。

q.q: Why is neutrino astronomy called a fresh 'window'?
opts: It reveals violent, hidden events that ordinary light cannot show us
It lets scientists see neutrinos with ordinary telescopes
q.why: 微中子能從光到不了的隱密劇烈之處帶來訊息，等於開了觀測宇宙的新窗。

discuss: Trillions of neutrinos pass right through you every second. Does knowing that change how you see the world?
IceCube was hugely expensive and sits in Antarctic ice. Is 'pure curiosity' science like this worth the cost? Why or why not?
Light, sound, and now neutrinos each tell us something about the universe. What new 'sense' might science invent next?

topic: Molecules with a Left Hand and a Right Hand
zh: 分子的左手與右手：2026 諾貝爾化學獎
tag: Nobel Chemistry · 諾貝爾化學獎

a.title: Molecules That Come in Two Hands
text: On October 7, 2026, two scientists won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Their names are Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai.
Hold up your two hands. They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right. You cannot put a left glove on your right hand.
Many tiny molecules are like this too. They come in a 'left' form and a 'right' form.
This really matters for medicine. Often only one hand helps your body. The other hand may do nothing — or even cause harm.
Kagan and Soai found clever ways to make mostly the hand we want. Soai even built a reaction that copies itself, turning a tiny difference into a big one.
Thanks to their work, chemists can make safer medicines, one careful hand at a time.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: Molecules that come in 'left' and 'right' forms, and a prize for making the one we want
Why left and right hands are mirror images
q.why: 全文講分子有「左手／右手」兩種形式，以及讓我們做出想要那一隻手的諾貝爾獎。

q.q: Why are a left and right hand like these molecules?
opts: They are mirror images that don't match up
q.why: 左右手是鏡像，無法完全重疊；這些分子也一樣。

q.q: Why does handedness matter for medicine?
opts: It changes the colour of pills
Often only one hand helps the body; the other may do nothing or cause harm
Both hands of a medicine always work in the same way
q.why: 通常只有一隻「手」對身體有效，另一隻可能無效或有害。

q.q: In the text, “harm” means ___.
q.why: harm ＝ 傷害。

q.q: Why is their work important?
opts: It helps chemists build safer medicines
q.why: 能讓化學家做出更安全的藥物。

gt.en: They look the same, but they are mirror images — a left and a right.
gt.zh: 它們看起來一樣，但其實是鏡像——一左一右。

gt.en: Many tiny molecules are like this too.
gt.zh: 許多微小的分子也是這樣。

gt.en: This really matters for medicine.
gt.zh: 這對醫藥來說真的非常重要。

gt.en: Soai even built a reaction that copies itself, turning a tiny difference into a big one.
gt.zh: 碩井甚至設計出一種會自我複製的反應，把微小的差異變成很大的差異。

b.title: Left-Handed and Right-Handed Molecules
text: On 7 October 2026, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri Kagan of France and Kenso Soai of Japan for work on 'asymmetric synthesis' — building molecules with a chosen handedness.
Just as your left and right hands are mirror images that cannot overlap, many molecules exist in two mirror-image forms, which chemists call 'left' and 'right'.
Inside living bodies, the two forms can behave completely differently. One form of a drug may heal, while its mirror twin does nothing — or causes side effects.
For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.
Kagan discovered that a small amount of a one-handed 'helper', called a catalyst, could steer a reaction to produce far more of a single form — a surprising amplifying effect.

Soai went further, creating a reaction that makes a product which then helps make more of itself. A tiny imbalance at the start grows into an almost perfectly one-handed result — a powerful tool for cleaner, safer medicines.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Kagan and Soai found ways to build molecules of a chosen 'handedness' — key to safer medicines — and won the 2026 Chemistry Nobel.
The two mirror forms of a drug can behave completely differently.
q.why: 核心：他們能做出指定「手性」的分子，對安全製藥很重要，獲 2026 化學獎。

q.q: In the body, the two mirror forms of a drug can ___.
q.why: 兩種鏡像在體內可能表現完全不同。

q.q: What did Soai's special reaction do?
opts: It made a product that helps make more of itself
It made both mirror forms faster than before
q.why: Soai 的反應會生成能幫助自己再生成的產物（自我催化）。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “amplifying” means ___.
q.why: amplify ＝ 放大、增強。

q.q: Why was making one single form hard before?
opts: Reactions usually made both forms equally, and separating them was slow and costly
q.why: 過去反應常同時產生兩種形式，分離既慢又貴。

tr.en: One form of a drug may heal, while its mirror twin does nothing — or causes side effects.
tr.zh: 一種藥物的某一種型態可能能治病，而它的鏡像雙胞胎卻沒有作用——甚至會造成副作用。

tr.en: For a long time, ordinary reactions made both forms in equal amounts, and separating them afterwards was slow and costly.
tr.zh: 很長一段時間，一般的化學反應會做出等量的兩種型態，而事後把它們分開既慢又昂貴。

tr.en: A tiny imbalance at the start grows into an almost perfectly one-handed result — a powerful tool for cleaner, safer medicines.
tr.zh: 一開始的微小不平衡，會擴大成幾乎完全單一手性的結果——這是製造更純淨、更安全藥物的強大工具。

c.title: The Chemistry of Handedness
text: When the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry on 7 October, it honoured Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for taming one of chemistry's most elegant puzzles: handedness.
Countless molecules are 'chiral' — they exist as two mirror images, like a pair of hands, that can never be laid perfectly on top of each other. The two versions are known as enantiomers.

In biology, the distinction is anything but trivial. The receptors in our cells are themselves handed, so one enantiomer of a drug may cure a patient while its mirror image is useless, or even dangerous.
Ordinary reactions, however, tend to produce the two forms in equal measure. The challenge was to tip the balance — to make one hand far more often than the other.

Kagan showed that this could be done with startling efficiency: a catalyst only slightly biased toward one hand could yield a product overwhelmingly of that hand, a counter-intuitive 'non-linear' effect.

Soai then revealed something close to chemical magic — a self-replicating, or autocatalytic, reaction in which the product speeds up its own formation, amplifying a faint initial imbalance into near-perfect purity. Together, their insights underpin the clean, precise synthesis of modern medicines.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: Why the two mirror forms of a drug behave differently in the body
How Kagan and Soai learned to control molecular 'handedness', earning the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
q.why: 全文講他們掌控分子手性、獲 2026 化學獎。

q.q: Why is handedness 'anything but trivial' in biology?
opts: Our receptors are themselves handed, so one enantiomer may cure while its mirror may harm
Cells are too small to matter
All molecules are the same hand
q.why: 細胞受體本身也有手性，所以一種鏡像可能有效、另一種可能有害。

q.q: What was Kagan's surprising 'non-linear' effect?
opts: A catalyst only slightly biased toward one hand could yield a product overwhelmingly of that hand
A catalyst had to be completely one-handed to make a one-handed product
q.why: 略偏一隻手的催化劑，卻能做出壓倒性偏向那隻手的產物。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “autocatalytic” describes a reaction that ___.
q.why: autocatalytic ＝ 自我催化：產物加速自身的生成。

q.q: Why does this chemistry matter beyond the laboratory?
opts: It underpins the clean, precise making of modern medicines
q.why: 它是現代藥物乾淨精準合成的基礎。

discuss: Your two hands are mirror images, yet not the same. Where else in nature or daily life do you notice 'handedness'?
One form of a molecule can heal while its mirror harms. Why is being precise so important in science and medicine?
Soai's reaction grows a tiny difference into a big one. Can you think of small starts in life that grow into big results?

topic: A Poet Who Bridges Ancient and Modern
zh: 連結古今的詩人：2026 諾貝爾文學獎
tag: Nobel Literature · 諾貝爾文學獎

a.title: A Poet Who Loves Old Stories
text: On October 8, 2026, the writer Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature. She is a poet from Canada.
Carson loves the stories and poems of ancient Greece, written thousands of years ago.
She takes these very old tales and tells them again in fresh, surprising, modern ways.
In one famous book, she retells a Greek myth about a small red monster — but as a tender story about growing up and falling in love.
Carson also teaches ancient Greek, and she has translated old poems so that people today can enjoy them.
The prize judges praised her bold and playful writing, which builds new shapes for poetry out of very old stories.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A poet who retells ancient Greek stories in modern ways, and the prize she won
q.why: 全文講一位把古希臘故事用現代方式重說的詩人，以及她得的諾貝爾獎。

q.q: Where is Anne Carson from?
opts: Greece, where the old stories come from
q.why: Anne Carson 是來自加拿大的詩人。

q.q: What does Carson do with ancient tales?
opts: She tells them again in fresh, modern ways
q.why: 她把古老故事用新鮮、現代的方式重新述說。

q.q: In the text, “ancient” means ___.
q.why: ancient ＝ 古老的、很久以前的。

q.q: Why did the judges praise her?
opts: She makes new kinds of poetry out of very old stories
q.why: 她用很古老的故事創造出新的詩歌形式。

gt.en: She is a poet from Canada.
gt.zh: 她是一位來自加拿大的詩人。

gt.en: Carson loves the stories and poems of ancient Greece, written thousands of years ago.
gt.zh: 卡森熱愛幾千年前寫成的古希臘故事和詩。

gt.zh: 卡森也教古希臘文，她還翻譯古老的詩，讓今天的人也能欣賞。

b.title: Anne Carson: New Shapes from Old Stories
text: On 8 October 2026, the Canadian poet Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature for work that brings the ancient world into playful, modern form.
Carson is both a poet and a scholar of ancient Greek. For her, writers who lived thousands of years ago — like the poet Sappho — are living voices, not dusty books.
Her most loved work, 'Autobiography of Red', takes a strange Greek myth about a winged red monster and turns it into a moving story about a shy boy growing up.
She refuses to stay inside one form. Her books mix poetry, essay, and story; one even unfolds like a long paper accordion.
She has also translated ancient poems, carefully keeping their gaps and silences so that readers feel how much time has passed.
The Nobel judges praised her 'bold and inventive' writing, which, in playful dialogue with the classics, has created new forms for today's literature.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Autobiography of Red retells a Greek myth about a red monster.
Anne Carson won the 2026 Literature Nobel for turning ancient Greek writing into bold, modern forms.
q.why: 核心：Carson 把古希臘文學化為大膽的現代形式，獲 2026 文學獎。

q.q: What is 'Autobiography of Red' about?
opts: A Greek myth about a winged red monster, retold as a boy growing up
q.why: 它把一個有翅膀紅怪物的希臘神話，改寫成男孩成長的故事。

q.q: How does Carson treat writers from thousands of years ago?
q.why: 她把古代作家當成「活著的聲音」，而非陳舊的書。

q.q: In paragraph 4, 'refuses to stay inside one form' means she ___.
q.why: 她不受單一文體限制，把詩、散文、故事混在一起。

q.q: Why keep the 'gaps and silences' in old poems?
opts: So readers feel how much time has passed
Because the ancient poems were never finished by their writers
q.why: 保留殘缺與留白，讓讀者感受到時間的久遠。

tr.en: Carson is both a poet and a scholar of ancient Greek.
tr.zh: 卡森既是詩人，也是研究古希臘文的學者。

tr.en: Her books mix poetry, essay, and story; one even unfolds like a long paper accordion.
tr.zh: 她的書混合了詩、散文和故事；其中一本甚至像一長條紙做的手風琴一樣展開。

tr.en: She has also translated ancient poems, carefully keeping their gaps and silences so that readers feel how much time has passed.
tr.zh: 她也翻譯古詩，小心地保留其中的缺漏與空白，讓讀者感受到時間已經過了多久。

c.title: In Playful Dialogue with the Ancients
text: When the Swedish Academy named Anne Carson the 2026 Nobel laureate in Literature on 8 October, it celebrated a writer who has spent her life in conversation with the distant past.
A Canadian poet, essayist, and professor of classics, Carson treats the ancient Greeks not as relics to be studied, but as companions to argue and play with.
Her signature work, 'Autobiography of Red', reimagines an obscure myth — the red, winged monster Geryon — as a luminous coming-of-age story written as a novel in verse.
Across her career she has dissolved the borders between genres, weaving together poetry, scholarship, and memoir; her elegy 'Nox' arrives as a single folded page in a box, part book, part object.
As a translator, she renders the surviving fragments of Sappho with their losses intact, letting the blank spaces speak as loudly as the words.

The Academy honoured her 'bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature' — proof that the oldest voices can still sound startlingly new.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How Anne Carson renews ancient literature in modern forms, earning the 2026 Nobel Prize
Why ancient Greek writers are still worth studying
q.why: 全文講 Carson 以現代形式更新古典文學，獲 2026 文學獎。

q.q: What is 'Nox' described as?
opts: A single folded page in a box, part book, part object
q.why: 〈Nox〉是裝在盒中、像手風琴般折疊的一張長頁，既是書也是物件。

q.q: How does Carson treat the ancient Greeks, according to the text?
opts: As companions to argue and play with
As great masters whose words should never be changed
q.why: 她把古希臘人當成可以爭辯、玩味的夥伴，而非只能研究的陳舊遺物。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “obscure” means ___.
q.why: obscure ＝ 冷僻的、不為人知的。

q.q: What does her win suggest about old stories?
opts: The oldest voices can still sound startlingly new
q.why: 最古老的聲音仍能煥發出驚人的新意。

discuss: Carson makes ancient stories feel new. Is there an old story, song, or legend you would love to retell in a modern way?
She mixes poetry, essay, and story in one book. Why might breaking the 'rules' of a form lead to something powerful?
Why do you think people still read writers who lived thousands of years ago?

topic: A Lifelong Fight for Human Rights
zh: 為人權奮鬥一生：2026 諾貝爾和平獎
tag: Nobel Peace · 諾貝爾和平獎

a.title: A Judge Who Fights for Fairness
text: On October 9, 2026, Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize. She is a judge and lawyer from South Africa.
Pillay grew up poor, at a time when her country treated people unfairly because of the colour of their skin.
She worked very hard, became a lawyer, and fought for people who had no voice.
Later, she became a judge in important world courts that try terrible crimes, such as war crimes.
She also led the part of the United Nations that protects human rights around the world.
The prize honours her long fight for peace and for fair laws that protect everyone, everywhere.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A trip to the United Nations
A judge who spent her life fighting for fairness and human rights
How the United Nations was started
q.why: 全文講一位一生為公平與人權奮鬥的法官。

q.q: Where is Navi Pillay from?
q.why: Navi Pillay 來自南非。

q.q: What did Pillay do at the United Nations?
opts: She led the part that protects human rights
q.why: 她領導聯合國負責保護人權的部門。

q.q: In the text, “unfair” means ___.
q.why: unfair ＝ 不公平、不公正。

q.q: Why did she win the Peace Prize?
opts: For her long fight for peace and fair laws that protect everyone
For ending apartheid in South Africa by herself
q.why: 因她長年為和平與保護所有人的公平法律而奮鬥。

gt.en: She is a judge and lawyer from South Africa.
gt.zh: 她是一位來自南非的法官和律師。

gt.en: She worked very hard, became a lawyer, and fought for people who had no voice.
gt.zh: 她非常努力，成為律師，並為沒有發聲機會的人奮鬥。

gt.en: Later, she became a judge in important world courts that try terrible crimes, such as war crimes.
gt.zh: 後來，她成為重要國際法庭的法官，審理像戰爭罪這樣可怕的罪行。

gt.en: She also led the part of the United Nations that protects human rights around the world.
gt.zh: 她也領導過聯合國中負責保護全世界人權的部門。

b.title: Navi Pillay: Justice Without Borders
text: On 9 October 2026, Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay of South Africa won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
Pillay was born into a poor family and grew up under apartheid, a cruel system that gave people different rights based on their race.
Against the odds, she studied law and became the first woman to open her own law practice in her province, defending people who were treated unjustly.
Her work later took her to the world stage. She served as a judge on international courts that hold leaders responsible for war crimes and genocide.
From 2008 to 2014, she led the United Nations office for human rights, speaking up for the vulnerable in every corner of the globe.
Her life shows that peace is built not only by stopping wars, but by building fair laws that protect the dignity of every person.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Navi Pillay won the 2026 Peace Prize for a lifetime promoting human rights and international law.
Navi Pillay was the first woman to open a law practice in her province.
q.why: 核心：Pillay 一生推動人權與國際法，獲 2026 和平獎。

q.q: What was apartheid?
opts: A cruel system that gave people different rights based on race
q.why: 種族隔離是依種族給予人們不同權利的殘酷制度。

q.q: What was Pillay the first woman to do in her province?
q.why: 她是該省第一位開設自己律師事務所的女性。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “vulnerable” means ___.
q.why: vulnerable ＝ 脆弱、易受傷害、需要保護的。

q.q: What does her life show about peace?
opts: Peace mainly means stopping wars between countries
Peace also means building fair laws that protect everyone's dignity
q.why: 和平不只是停止戰爭，也是建立保護每個人尊嚴的公平法律。

tr.en: Pillay was born into a poor family and grew up under apartheid, a cruel system that gave people different rights based on their race.
tr.zh: 皮萊出生在貧窮的家庭，在種族隔離制度下長大——那是一個依照種族給人不同權利的殘酷制度。

tr.en: She served as a judge on international courts that hold leaders responsible for war crimes and genocide.
tr.zh: 她曾在國際法庭擔任法官，這些法庭追究領導人在戰爭罪和種族滅絕上的責任。

tr.en: From 2008 to 2014, she led the United Nations office for human rights, speaking up for the vulnerable in every corner of the globe.
tr.zh: 從 2008 年到 2014 年，她領導聯合國人權事務辦公室，為全球每個角落的弱勢者發聲。

c.title: Building Peace Through Law
text: When the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the 2026 Peace Prize to Navi Pillay on 9 October, it recognised a lifetime spent insisting that justice belongs to everyone, not only the powerful.

Born in 1941 into a working-class family in South Africa, Pillay came of age under apartheid, a system that stripped most of the population of basic rights. Education became her way out — and her weapon.
She became the first non-white woman to open a law practice in her province, often defending opponents of the regime when few others dared.

Her reach grew global. As a judge, and later president, of the international tribunal for Rwanda, she helped establish that rape could be prosecuted as a crime of genocide — a landmark for international justice.
From 2008 to 2014 she served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, a fearless voice for the persecuted regardless of politics or borders.
Her career embodies a quiet but radical idea: that lasting peace rests on the rule of law, and that protecting the rights of the weakest protects us all.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: Why the Rwanda tribunal was a landmark for international law
How Navi Pillay built peace through law and human rights, earning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
q.why: 全文講 Pillay 以法律與人權建立和平，獲 2026 和平獎。

q.q: What landmark did Pillay help establish at the Rwanda tribunal?
opts: That rape could be prosecuted as a crime of genocide
q.why: 她協助確立：強暴可被當作種族滅絕罪起訴，是國際司法的里程碑。

q.q: What role did she hold from 2008 to 2014?
opts: United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights
q.why: 2008–2014 年她擔任聯合國人權事務高級專員。

q.q: In paragraph 2, education is called her 'way out — and her weapon.' This means education ___.
opts: helped her escape poverty and fight injustice
q.why: 教育既是她脫離貧困的出路，也是對抗不公的武器。

q.q: What 'radical idea' does her career embody?
opts: Peace comes mainly from strong leaders, not from laws
Lasting peace rests on the rule of law and on protecting the weakest
q.why: 持久的和平建立在法治之上，保護最弱者就是保護所有人。

discuss: Pillay said education was her 'way out.' How can learning change a person's whole life?
She believed that protecting the weakest protects everyone. Do you agree? Why or why not?
What is one unfair thing in the world you would fight to change — and how might you start?

topic: Pompeii: The City Frozen in Time
zh: 龐貝：凝固在時間裡的城市

a.title: The City the Volcano Buried
text: Pompeii was a busy Roman city in Italy, almost two thousand years ago. People lived, worked, and shopped there every day.
Near the city stood a mountain called Mount Vesuvius. The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.
In the year 79, the volcano erupted. It threw ash and rock high into the sky for two days.
The whole city was buried under deep ash. Sadly, many people could not escape in time.
For hundreds of years, Pompeii lay hidden and forgotten. Then, much later, people dug it up again.
Today we can walk through its streets and houses. Pompeii shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why Mount Vesuvius is a dangerous volcano
A Roman city buried by a volcano and found again
q.why: 全文講龐貝這座羅馬城被火山掩埋、後來又被挖掘出來。

q.q: What was Mount Vesuvius?
q.why: 第二段：a dangerous volcano。

q.q: What happened to the city in the year 79?
opts: Everyone escaped before the ash came
q.why: 第三、四段：火山爆發，整座城被深厚的火山灰掩埋。

q.q: In the text, “erupt” means a volcano ___.
opts: suddenly throws out ash, rock, and fire
q.why: erupt =（火山）爆發，噴出火山灰、岩石與火。

q.q: Why is Pompeii special today?
opts: It shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago
It is the newest city in Italy
No one is allowed to visit
q.why: 末段：Pompeii shows us exactly how Romans lived long ago。

gt.en: Pompeii was a busy Roman city in Italy, almost two thousand years ago.
gt.zh: 龐貝是將近兩千年前義大利一座熱鬧的羅馬城市。

gt.en: The people did not know it was a dangerous volcano.
gt.zh: 人們不知道那是一座危險的火山。

gt.en: In the year 79, the volcano erupted.
gt.zh: 西元 79 年，火山爆發了。

gt.en: The whole city was buried under deep ash.
gt.zh: 整座城市被埋在厚厚的火山灰下。

b.title: A Day That Stopped Forever
text: Nearly two thousand years ago, Pompeii was a lively Roman town near the bay of Naples, in Italy — home to shops, baths, theatres, and around twelve thousand people.
Looming above it was Mount Vesuvius. Few people realised that the green mountain was in fact a sleeping volcano.
In AD 79, Vesuvius exploded with terrible force. For two days it rained ash and burning rock, until the town — and many who had stayed behind — lay buried under metres of volcanic debris.
Terrible as it was, the ash also preserved the city. Buildings, wall paintings, loaves of bread, and even the shapes of people were sealed and protected underground for centuries.
Rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward, Pompeii became a window into the ancient world. Archaeologists could read shop signs, study homes, and learn what Romans ate and wore.
Vesuvius is still active today, and scientists watch it closely. Pompeii remains a haunting reminder of nature's power — and a priceless record of a single ancient day.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: A volcano destroyed Pompeii in AD 79, but the ash preserved it as a record of Roman life.
q.why: 核心：火山摧毀龐貝，但火山灰保存了它，成為羅馬生活的紀錄。

q.q: About how many people lived in Pompeii?
q.why: 第一段：around twelve thousand people。

q.q: How did the ash help, despite the disaster?
opts: It sealed and preserved buildings and objects underground
It made the soil rich, so the city was rebuilt quickly
q.why: 第四段：the ash also preserved the city…sealed and protected underground。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “excavated” means ___.
opts: carefully dug out of the ground
q.why: excavate = 挖掘出土；考古學家把龐貝從地底慢慢挖出來。

q.q: Why is Pompeii called “a window into the ancient world”?
opts: It can only be seen from the sky
Its preserved streets and objects let us see how Romans really lived
q.why: 被保存的街道與物件讓我們直接看見古羅馬人的真實生活，如同一扇觀看古代的窗。

tr.en: Few people realised that the green mountain was in fact a sleeping volcano.
tr.zh: 很少人意識到，那座綠色的山其實是一座沉睡的火山。

tr.en: Terrible as it was, the ash also preserved the city.
tr.zh: 雖然這場災難很可怕，火山灰卻也把這座城市保存了下來。

tr.en: Rediscovered and slowly excavated from the 1700s onward, Pompeii became a window into the ancient world.
tr.zh: 從十八世紀起重新被發現並慢慢挖掘出來，龐貝成了一扇通往古代世界的窗。

c.title: The Gift of Catastrophe
text: Among the ironies of history, few are sharper than Pompeii: a catastrophe that destroyed a city and, in the same stroke, saved it. When Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, it ended thousands of lives; it also sealed an entire Roman town beneath a blanket of ash, pausing it, mid-gesture, for nearly two millennia.

What makes Pompeii extraordinary is not grandeur but ordinariness. Rome left behind temples and monuments by design; Pompeii left behind the unguarded everyday — graffiti scratched on walls, election posters, a dog chained in a doorway, a meal abandoned on a table. The eruption froze not emperors but ordinary people, caught in an ordinary morning.

The ash proved a cruel kind of preservative. By packing tightly around bodies that later decayed, it left hollow moulds; when archaeologists poured plaster into these voids, the victims' final postures emerged — figures crouching, shielding children, holding one another.
Such discoveries raise uneasy questions about how we study the dead. Pompeii is at once a scientific treasure and a mass grave, and the line between learning and intrusion is not always clear.
Still, the town endures as our most vivid link to antiquity — proof that the smallest details of a vanished life can outlast the empires that once seemed so much more permanent.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central idea?
opts: Pompeii is a disaster that, by destroying a city, also preserved it as a uniquely ordinary record of the past.
Pompeii shows that volcano disasters destroy everything they touch.
q.why: 開頭的反諷即主旨：一場毀滅城市的災難，同時把它保存成最平凡卻珍貴的歷史紀錄。

q.q: In paragraph 2, the writer says Pompeii's value is “not grandeur but ordinariness,” meaning its worth lies in ___.
opts: the ordinary, everyday details of real lives
q.why: grandeur（宏偉）對比 ordinariness（平凡）：龐貝珍貴之處在於塗鴉、選舉海報、餐桌等日常細節。

q.q: How were the famous body shapes of victims created?
opts: They are Roman statues found in the ash
Plaster was poured into hollow moulds the decayed bodies left in the ash
q.why: 第三段：遺體腐化後在火山灰中留下空腔，考古學家灌入石膏，還原出罹難者最後的姿態。

q.q: What tension does paragraph 4 raise?
opts: That Pompeii is both a scientific treasure and a mass grave, so studying it can feel like intrusion
q.why: 第四段點出矛盾：龐貝既是科學寶藏，也是集體墳墓，研究與冒犯之間界線模糊。

q.q: The whole essay is framed around ___.
opts: an irony: destruction that also preserved
q.why: 全文以「摧毀同時也保存」的反諷貫穿（首段提出、末段呼應）。

discuss: Why do you think people today are so fascinated by Pompeii?
Pompeii is both a scientific treasure and a mass grave. Should human remains be shown to the public? Why or why not?
If a city today were suddenly frozen in time, what everyday objects would best tell the future about us?

topic: Kyoto: Japan's Ancient Capital
zh: 京都：日本的千年古都
src: The New York Times · National Geographic · Taipei Times

a.title: Welcome to Kyoto
text: Kyoto is a beautiful old city in Japan. For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.
Kyoto is famous for its temples and shrines. Some are made of wood and are very, very old.
One famous place is Fushimi Inari, where thousands of bright orange gates stand in a long line up a hill.
In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the city. In autumn, the leaves turn red and gold. Many people visit just to see them.
In the old streets of Gion, you might see a geisha in a beautiful kimono walking quietly by.
Kyoto mixes the old and the new. It is a wonderful place to learn about Japanese history and culture.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A beautiful old Japanese city and what to see there
Why Kyoto was Japan's capital for a thousand years
q.why: 全文介紹京都這座古城與值得一看的景點。

q.q: What was Kyoto for more than a thousand years?
q.why: 第一段：for more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital。

q.q: What is famous about Fushimi Inari?
opts: Thousands of bright orange gates up a hill
q.why: 第三段：thousands of bright orange gates…up a hill。

q.q: In the text, a “shrine” is ___.
opts: a holy place where people pray
q.why: shrine = 神社，供人參拜的神聖之地。

q.q: Why do many people visit Kyoto in spring and autumn?
opts: Because it is the cheapest time
To see the cherry blossoms and the red autumn leaves
Because the temples are only open in spring and autumn
q.why: 第四段：春天櫻花、秋天紅黃落葉，很多人專程來看。

gt.en: For more than a thousand years, it was the country's capital.
gt.zh: 一千多年來，它都是這個國家的首都。

gt.en: Kyoto is famous for its temples and shrines.
gt.zh: 京都以它的寺廟和神社聞名。

gt.en: In spring, pink cherry blossoms cover the city.
gt.zh: 春天時，粉紅色的櫻花覆蓋整座城市。

gt.en: In the old streets of Gion, you might see a geisha in a beautiful kimono walking quietly by.
gt.zh: 在祇園的老街上，你可能會看到一位穿著美麗和服的藝妓靜靜地走過。

b.title: A City of a Thousand Years
text: For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan. Though Tokyo holds that title now, Kyoto remains the nation's cultural heart.

The city is home to around two thousand temples and shrines. At Kiyomizu-dera, a wooden hall stands on tall pillars over a hillside; at Fushimi Inari, thousands of vermilion gates form glowing tunnels up the mountain.
Kyoto changes beautifully with the seasons. Spring brings clouds of cherry blossom; autumn sets the maples of Arashiyama ablaze in red and orange. These two seasons draw by far the largest crowds.
The old district of Gion is famous for its wooden tea houses and its geisha, women trained for years in traditional dance, music, and the art of conversation.
Visitors can still enjoy a simple cup of matcha tea, a quiet temple garden, or a meal of local tofu and vegetables.
Above all, Kyoto asks to be taken slowly. It rewards those who wander its back streets and pause to notice small, carefully made beauty.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Kyoto is a modern business city.
Kyoto, Japan's old capital, is a seasonal, cultural city best enjoyed slowly.
q.why: 核心：京都是日本古都、充滿四季與文化之美，最適合慢慢品味。

q.q: Until what year was Kyoto the capital of Japan?
q.why: 第一段：until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan。

q.q: What is the Gion district known for?
q.why: 第四段：Gion is famous for its wooden tea houses and its geisha。

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “district” is ___.
opts: an area or part of a city
q.why: district = （城市的）區、地段。

q.q: What does “Kyoto asks to be taken slowly” suggest?
opts: You appreciate Kyoto best by slowing down and noticing details
Visitors should spend most of their time at the famous sites
q.why: 末段：放慢腳步、留意細節的人，最能體會京都的美。

tr.en: For over a thousand years, until 1868, Kyoto was the capital of Japan.
tr.zh: 一千多年來，直到 1868 年，京都都是日本的首都。

tr.en: These two seasons draw by far the largest crowds.
tr.zh: 這兩個季節吸引的人潮是最多的。

tr.en: It rewards those who wander its back streets and pause to notice small, carefully made beauty.
tr.zh: 它會回報那些在小巷裡漫步、停下來欣賞細膩之美的人。

c.title: The Art of Going Slowly
text: To arrive in Kyoto expecting a museum is to misread it. Japan's capital for more than a millennium, the city wears its history not as a relic under glass but as a living habit — in the rhythm of its seasons, the manners of its streets, and a quiet insistence on doing things with care.

Its set-piece treasures are rightly famous: the vermilion corridors of Fushimi Inari, the hillside stage of Kiyomizu-dera, the towering bamboo groves of Arashiyama. Yet the first-time visitor, hurrying between them with a guidebook, often misses what makes Kyoto itself — the unhurried attention it pays to small things.

That attention shows everywhere: in a bowl of tea whisked just so, in a raked gravel garden meant to be contemplated rather than entered, in the training of a geisha measured not in weeks but in years.
Modern Kyoto, of course, also has traffic, convenience stores, and crowds that strain its most delicate corners, raising hard questions about how a living city can carry so priceless a past.
Perhaps that is Kyoto's deepest lesson for the traveller — and a useful one anywhere: that beauty is often found not by seeing more, but by slowing down enough to notice what was already there.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Kyoto is just an open-air museum.
Kyoto's beauty is mainly in its famous temples and shrines.
Only famous sites in Kyoto matter.
Kyoto is a living city whose real beauty is found by slowing down and paying attention.
q.why: 主旨：京都是座「活著」的城市，其真正之美在於放慢腳步、用心留意。

q.q: In paragraph 1, a “relic under glass” is used to describe what Kyoto is NOT — meaning Kyoto's history is ___.
opts: alive and part of daily life
q.why: 作者說京都不是玻璃櫃裡的遺物（relic），而是「活的習慣」——歷史融入日常。

q.q: What do hurried first-time visitors tend to miss?
opts: The unhurried attention Kyoto pays to small things
The famous sites, because they are too crowded to enter
q.why: 第二段：趕景點的遊客，反而錯過了京都真正的特質——對小事的從容用心。

q.q: What does paragraph 4 add to the essay?
opts: It honestly admits modern strains (traffic, crowds) on a fragile, priceless city
q.why: 第四段坦承現代京都也有交通、人潮等壓力，讓讚美更真實平衡。

q.q: How does the writer mainly develop the piece?
opts: By comparing Kyoto to Tokyo only
By contrasting rushing between sights with slowing down to notice detail
q.why: 全文以「趕景點 vs 放慢留意細節」的對比推進，最後收束成普遍的人生體會。

discuss: Would you rather travel to see as much as possible, or slow down and experience a few places deeply? Why?
Kyoto struggles with too many tourists. How can a city protect its culture and still welcome visitors?
Think of a place in Taiwan that mixes old and new. How would you introduce it to a foreign friend in English?

topic: How to Keep a Whole Economy Steady
zh: 如何穩住整個經濟：2026 諾貝爾經濟獎
tag: Nobel Economics · 諾貝爾經濟獎

a.title: Keeping Prices and Jobs Steady
text: On October 12, 2026, two economists won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. Their names are Robert Hall and Michael Woodford.
An economy is all the buying, selling, saving, and working in a country.
Sometimes prices rise too fast, so money buys less. Sometimes many people lose their jobs. Both are big problems.
Countries have special banks, called central banks, that try to keep prices and jobs steady.
Hall and Woodford studied how the small choices of ordinary people and shops add up to the whole economy.
Their ideas help central banks choose good actions — like changing interest rates — to calm prices and help people keep working.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: How to change interest rates at a central bank
Two economists who studied how to keep prices and jobs steady
q.why: 全文講兩位研究如何穩住物價與就業的經濟學家。

q.q: What do central banks try to do?
q.why: 中央銀行設法讓物價與就業保持穩定。

q.q: What did Hall and Woodford study?
opts: How small choices of people and shops add up to the whole economy
q.why: 他們研究一般人與商店的小選擇如何加總成整個經濟。

q.q: In the text, “steady” means ___.
q.why: steady ＝ 穩定、不會變動太大。

q.q: Why are their ideas useful?
opts: They help central banks choose good actions, like changing interest rates
They let central banks control every price in the shops
q.why: 幫助中央銀行選擇好的做法，如調整利率。

gt.en: An economy is all the buying, selling, saving, and working in a country.
gt.zh: 經濟就是一個國家裡所有的買、賣、儲蓄和工作。

gt.en: Sometimes prices rise too fast, so money buys less.
gt.zh: 有時候物價漲得太快，錢就買得到比較少的東西。

gt.en: Countries have special banks, called central banks, that try to keep prices and jobs steady.
gt.zh: 各國都有特別的銀行，叫做中央銀行，它們努力讓物價和就業保持穩定。

b.title: The Science of a Stable Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on the 'microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.
That long phrase hides a simple question: how do the everyday choices of millions of people and businesses add up to the ups and downs of a whole country's economy?
When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs. Governments want to avoid both.
Hall and Woodford built careful models showing how people's spending, saving, and especially their expectations about the future shape the bigger picture.
Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.
Because of ideas like theirs, the banks that guard our money can act with more confidence when they try to keep prices stable and jobs plentiful.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Central banks use interest rates to keep prices from rising too fast.
Hall and Woodford won the 2026 Economics Nobel for showing how everyday choices shape a whole economy, helping central banks keep it stable.
q.why: 核心：他們說明日常選擇如何形塑整體經濟，助中央銀行維持穩定，獲 2026 經濟獎。

q.q: What two problems do governments want to avoid?
opts: Prices rising too fast, and many people losing their jobs
q.why: 物價漲太快與大量失業，都是政府想避免的問題。

q.q: Besides spending and saving, what especially shapes the big picture?
opts: How much money the central bank prints
q.why: 人們對未來的「預期」特別影響整體經濟。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “steer” means ___.
q.why: steer ＝ 駕馭、引導方向。

q.q: Why does their work give central banks 'more confidence'?
opts: It gives a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates
q.why: 提供更穩固的理論基礎，讓央行更有把握地運用利率等工具。

tr.en: When prices rise too quickly, savings lose value; when demand falls, factories close and workers lose their jobs.
tr.zh: 物價上漲太快時，存款就會貶值；需求下降時，工廠關門，工人失業。

tr.en: Hall and Woodford built careful models showing how people's spending, saving, and especially their expectations about the future shape the bigger picture.
tr.zh: 霍爾和伍德福德建立了嚴謹的模型，說明人們的消費、儲蓄，特別是他們對未來的預期，如何影響整體的經濟。

tr.en: Their work gave central banks a firmer basis for using tools like interest rates to steer the economy between overheating and slowing down.
tr.zh: 他們的研究讓中央銀行在運用利率等工具、讓經濟在過熱與放緩之間保持平衡時，有了更穩固的依據。

c.title: From Small Choices to the Whole Economy
text: On 12 October 2026, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford 'for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation'.

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole — inflation, unemployment, growth — while microeconomics studies the decisions of single households and firms. The laureates helped bind the two together.

Their central insight is that the great swings of a national economy grow out of countless individual choices: how much to spend or save, what prices to set, and above all, what people expect to happen next.
Woodford showed how a central bank's words and credibility shape those expectations, so that guiding what people believe about future inflation can be as powerful as any single change in rates.
Hall illuminated how labour markets and spending respond over the business cycle, clarifying why recessions deepen and how recoveries take hold.

Together, their rigorous models turned central banking from something of an art into something far closer to a science, underpinning how institutions today fight both runaway prices and painful slumps.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How central banks use interest rates to fight inflation
How Hall and Woodford linked individual choices to whole-economy stability, earning the 2026 Economics Nobel
q.why: 全文講他們把個人選擇與整體經濟穩定連結，獲 2026 經濟獎。

q.q: How do macroeconomics and microeconomics differ?
opts: Macro studies the whole economy; micro studies single households and firms
q.why: 總體經濟學研究整體；個體經濟學研究單一家庭與廠商。

q.q: What did Woodford show about a central bank?
opts: It should keep its plans secret so markets are surprised
Its words and credibility shape people's expectations
q.why: 央行的言論與可信度會形塑人們的預期。

q.q: In paragraph 6, “slumps” most nearly means ___.
q.why: slump ＝ 經濟下滑、衰退。

q.q: Why is central banking now 'closer to a science'?
opts: Rigorous models guide how they fight both inflation and recessions
q.why: 嚴謹的模型指引央行同時對抗通膨與衰退。

discuss: When prices rise quickly, what changes do you notice in your family's daily life?
The laureates say our 'expectations about the future' shape the economy. Can expecting something make it more likely to happen?
If you ran a central bank, would you focus more on stable prices or on more jobs? Why?

topic: Iceland: The Land of Fire and Ice
zh: 冰島：冰與火之地
src: National Geographic · The New York Times · Nature

a.title: Welcome to Iceland
text: Iceland is a small island country in the north Atlantic Ocean. It is famous for fire and ice.
The land has many volcanoes. It also has huge glaciers — slow rivers of thick ice.
Hot water bubbles up from under the ground. People relax in warm pools, even when snow is falling around them.
In winter, you can sometimes see the northern lights — green and pink lights dancing in the night sky.
Iceland has waterfalls, black sand beaches, and tall cliffs full of seabirds called puffins.
The capital city is Reykjavik. From there, visitors drive out to explore one of the most beautiful lands on Earth.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How to swim in the ocean
How to see the northern lights in winter
q.why: 全文介紹冰島及其驚人的自然景觀。

q.q: Iceland is famous for ___.
q.why: 第一段：famous for fire and ice。

q.q: When can you sometimes see the northern lights?
q.why: 第四段：In winter, you can sometimes see the northern lights。

q.q: In the text, a “glacier” is ___.
opts: a huge, slow-moving river of ice
q.why: glacier = 冰川，緩慢移動的巨大冰體。

q.q: Why can people relax in warm pools even in the snow?
opts: The sun heats the water even in winter
The pools are heated by hot water from under the ground
q.why: 第三段：地底冒出的熱水讓水池溫暖，即使周圍下雪也能泡。

gt.en: Iceland is a small island country in the north Atlantic Ocean.
gt.zh: 冰島是北大西洋上的一個小島國。

gt.en: The land has many volcanoes.
gt.zh: 這片土地上有許多火山。

gt.en: Hot water bubbles up from under the ground.
gt.zh: 熱水從地底下冒出來。

gt.en: Iceland has waterfalls, black sand beaches, and tall cliffs full of seabirds called puffins.
gt.zh: 冰島有瀑布、黑沙灘，還有布滿海鸚這種海鳥的高聳懸崖。

b.title: Where the Earth Is Still Being Made
text: Few countries feel as otherworldly as Iceland, a volcanic island near the Arctic Circle where fire and ice share the same landscape.
The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common. At the same time, vast glaciers cover much of the interior.
This restless geology is also a gift. Heat from underground warms homes and fills open-air pools such as the famous Blue Lagoon, even in freezing weather.
Nature is never far away. The 'Golden Circle' route takes visitors past a thundering waterfall, erupting hot springs, and a rift valley where two continents slowly split.
In the long winter nights, the sky sometimes glows with the aurora — curtains of green and violet light; in summer, by contrast, the sun barely sets at all.
With a tiny population and enormous open spaces, Iceland offers travellers something rare: the chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Iceland is a volcanic island where fire and ice meet, offering travellers the raw power of nature.
The Blue Lagoon is warmed by heat from underground.
q.why: 核心：冰島是冰火交會的火山島，讓旅人近距離感受自然的原始力量。

q.q: Why are volcanoes and earthquakes common in Iceland?
opts: It is very hot all year
It sits close to the North Pole
It sits where two of Earth's plates pull apart
q.why: 第二段：two of Earth's great plates pull apart。

q.q: What warms the Blue Lagoon and many homes?
q.why: 第三段：Heat from underground warms homes and fills open-air pools。

q.q: In paragraph 5, the “aurora” is ___.
opts: coloured lights that glow in the night sky
q.why: aurora = 極光，夜空中閃動的彩色光幕。

q.q: What does the writer say is “rare” about visiting Iceland?
opts: The chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close
q.why: 末段：the chance to feel the raw power of the planet up close。

tr.en: Few countries feel as otherworldly as Iceland, a volcanic island near the Arctic Circle where fire and ice share the same landscape.
tr.zh: 很少有國家像冰島一樣讓人覺得不像在地球上——這座靠近北極圈的火山島，火與冰共享同一片風景。

tr.en: The island sits where two of Earth's great plates pull apart, so volcanoes and earthquakes are common.
tr.zh: 這座島位在地球兩大板塊分開的地方，所以火山和地震很常見。

tr.en: The 'Golden Circle' route takes visitors past a thundering waterfall, erupting hot springs, and a rift valley where two continents slowly split.
tr.zh: 「黃金圈」路線帶遊客經過轟隆作響的瀑布、噴發的溫泉，還有兩塊大陸慢慢分開的裂谷。

c.title: Living on the Seam of the World
text: To travel in Iceland is to be reminded, constantly, that the ground beneath us is alive. The island straddles the boundary between two tectonic plates, and so it is forever being torn apart and built anew — a country, in effect, under construction.

This gives the landscape its strange grandeur: lava fields still black and bare, geysers that fire boiling water skyward, glaciers grinding whole valleys into shape. It also gives Icelanders a practical bargain with the earth, drawing clean heat and power from the volcanic rock below.

That intimacy with nature shapes the culture. A nation of fewer than four hundred thousand people has produced a fierce literary tradition, a deep love of storytelling, and — famously — a lingering half-seriousness about elves said to live in the rocks.

Tourism, now vital to the economy, brings its own tensions: fragile moss and quiet places can be worn away by too many feet, and Icelanders openly debate how to welcome the world without losing what makes the island special.
Still, few places teach the traveller so plainly that the planet is not a fixed stage but a living, moving thing — and that we are, all of us, only its temporary guests.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Iceland is a quiet, unchanging place.
Iceland's living, shifting land shapes its culture and reminds travellers we are only temporary guests on a moving planet.
Iceland's culture is mainly built on its belief in elves.
q.why: 主旨：不斷變動的大地形塑了冰島文化，也提醒旅人——我們只是這顆活著星球上的過客。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “straddles the boundary between two tectonic plates” means Iceland ___.
opts: sits across the line where two plates meet
q.why: straddle = 橫跨；冰島跨在兩大板塊的交界上。

q.q: How does the land shape Icelandic culture, according to the text?
opts: It feeds storytelling, literature, and even folk beliefs about elves
It makes people afraid to tell stories about nature
q.why: 第三段：與自然的親近孕育了文學傳統、說故事的熱愛，甚至對岩中精靈的半認真信念。

q.q: What tension does paragraph 4 add?
opts: Tourism is vital but can wear away fragile places, so Icelanders debate how to manage it
q.why: 第四段坦承觀光重要卻會磨損脆弱之地，冰島人正辯論該如何平衡。

q.q: How does the essay progress?
opts: From a menu to a bill
From a poem to a song
From the living land, to how it shapes culture, to tourism's tension, to a closing lesson
From a map to a ticket
q.why: 結構：活的大地 → 形塑文化 → 觀光的張力 → 收束於人生體會。

discuss: Iceland gets clean energy from volcanoes. How else could countries use nature's power safely?
Too many tourists can damage fragile places. How should a country balance tourism and protection?
Would you rather travel for a place's nature or its cities? Why?

topic: A Rover Plans Its Own Path on Mars
zh: 火星車自己規劃路線：AI 開上火星

a.title: A Robot Driver on Mars
text: On Mars, a NASA robot car called Perseverance explores a dry, rocky world far from Earth.
Mars is about 140 million miles away. A message from Earth takes many minutes to arrive.
Because of this delay, drivers on Earth cannot steer the rover in real time.
In December 2025, something new happened. For the first time, artificial intelligence — AI — planned the rover's path by itself.
The AI looked at pictures of the ground taken from space. It found rocks, sand, and safe places to drive, then drew a route.
The rover followed the plan and drove hundreds of metres. NASA shared the exciting results in January 2026.

q.q: What is the text mainly about?
opts: A rover on Mars drove a route planned by AI
Why messages take many minutes to reach Mars
q.why: 火星車 Perseverance 走了一條由 AI 規劃的路線。

q.q: Why can't drivers on Earth steer the rover live?
opts: Mars is so far that messages take many minutes
q.why: 火星太遠，訊息要好幾分鐘才到，無法即時操控。

q.q: What did the AI look at to plan the route?
opts: Pictures of the ground taken from space
q.why: AI 看從太空拍的地面照片來規劃路線。

q.q: In the text, “delay” means ___.
opts: a time when something is late
q.why: delay ＝ 延遲、慢了的時間。

q.q: Why is this a big deal?
opts: For the first time, AI planned the path by itself
For the first time, the rover drove on Mars
q.why: 這是第一次由 AI 自己規劃路線，所以意義重大。

gt.en: On Mars, a NASA robot car called Perseverance explores a dry, rocky world far from Earth.
gt.zh: 在火星上，一輛叫做毅力號的 NASA 機器車在離地球很遠、乾燥多岩石的世界裡探險。

gt.en: Because of this delay, drivers on Earth cannot steer the rover in real time.
gt.zh: 因為這個延遲，地球上的駕駛員無法即時操控探測車。

gt.en: It found rocks, sand, and safe places to drive, then drew a route.
gt.zh: 它找出岩石、沙子和可以安全行駛的地方，然後畫出一條路線。

b.title: AI Takes the Wheel on Mars
text: In December 2025, NASA's Perseverance rover did something no spacecraft had done before: it drove along a route planned entirely by artificial intelligence. NASA announced the results in January 2026.
Driving on Mars is tricky. The planet is about 225 million kilometres away, so radio signals take many minutes each way. Steering the rover live from Earth is impossible.
For 28 years, human engineers have carefully sketched each route by hand, marking points where the rover stops to receive new instructions.

This time, a kind of generative AI studied high-resolution photos taken from orbit, together with maps of the slopes. It recognised bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand, then designed a smooth path.
Before sending the plan to Mars, engineers tested it on a 'digital twin' — a virtual copy of the rover — checking hundreds of thousands of details.
The rover then rolled safely across Jezero Crater. One day, AI could let explorers on other worlds make quick decisions on their own.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: For the first time, generative AI planned a safe driving route for NASA's Perseverance rover on Mars.
Engineers tested the route on a digital twin of the rover.
q.why: 核心：首次由生成式 AI 為火星車規劃安全路線。

q.q: How did engineers check the plan before using it?
opts: They tested it on a 'digital twin', a virtual copy of the rover
q.why: 他們先在「數位分身」（虛擬火星車）上測試。

q.q: What did the AI recognise in the images?
opts: Bedrock, boulders, and ripples of sand
q.why: AI 辨認出岩床、巨石與沙紋。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “recognised” means ___.
opts: identified or knew what something was
q.why: recognise ＝ 辨認出。

q.q: Why might AI driving matter for the future?
opts: Explorers and robots on other worlds could make quick decisions on their own
Humans will no longer need to check any robot's plans
q.why: 未來其他星球上的機器人或太空人能更自主地即時決定。

tr.en: In December 2025, NASA's Perseverance rover did something no spacecraft had done before: it drove along a route planned entirely by artificial intelligence.
tr.zh: 2025 年 12 月，NASA 的毅力號探測車做了一件從來沒有太空船做過的事：它沿著一條完全由人工智慧規劃的路線行駛。

tr.en: The planet is about 225 million kilometres away, so radio signals take many minutes each way.
tr.zh: 這顆行星大約在兩億兩千五百萬公里外，所以無線電訊號單程就要好幾分鐘。

tr.en: For 28 years, human engineers have carefully sketched each route by hand, marking points where the rover stops to receive new instructions.
tr.zh: 二十八年來，人類工程師都是用手仔細畫出每一條路線，標出探測車要停下來接收新指令的地點。

c.title: When a Rover Plans Its Own Path
text: In January 2026, NASA revealed a quiet milestone in space exploration: the previous December, its Perseverance rover had completed the first drives on another world mapped out not by people, but by artificial intelligence.

The challenge is distance. With Mars roughly 225 million kilometres from Earth, radio commands arrive many minutes late, making real-time control impossible. For nearly three decades, engineers have plotted every route by hand, waypoint by waypoint.
The new approach used a form of generative AI known as vision-language models. The system examined sharp images from a Mars orbiter and detailed maps of the terrain's slopes.
From that data it identified bedrock, boulder fields, and ripples of sand, then stitched together a continuous, safe path — spacing its waypoints far more widely than human planners usually dare.
Nothing was sent blindly. The commands were first rehearsed on a 'digital twin', a virtual replica of the rover, where engineers checked over half a million measurements.
The drives, covering several hundred metres across Jezero Crater, hint at a future in which distant robots — and perhaps astronauts — navigate strange landscapes with far less help from home.

q.q: What is the passage mainly about?
opts: How NASA's Perseverance rover drove a route planned by AI, and why that matters
How engineers have planned rover routes by hand for thirty years
q.why: 全文講火星車走 AI 規劃的路線及其意義。

q.q: For how long have engineers plotted rover routes by hand?
q.why: 工程師以人工規劃路線已近三十年。

q.q: How did the AI's waypoints differ from human ones?
opts: They were spaced far more widely than human planners usually dare
They were placed exactly where human planners would put them
q.why: AI 的路徑點間距比人工規劃大得多。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “rehearsed” most nearly means ___.
q.why: rehearse ＝ 事先預演。

q.q: What does the drive 'hint at'?
opts: A future where distant robots and astronauts navigate with less help from Earth
q.why: 暗示未來遠方的機器人與太空人能更少依賴地球導航。

discuss: Would you trust an AI to plan your path if no one could fix its mistakes for twenty minutes? Why or why not?
Humans planned Mars routes for 28 years. What is gained — and what might be lost — when AI takes over the job?
Where else could machines that 'plan for themselves' help people here on Earth?

topic: The Fall of the Berlin Wall
zh: 柏林圍牆倒塌
src: The New York Times · The Economist · BBC

a.title: The Night the Wall Came Down
text: For 28 years, a long concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two. On one side was East Germany; on the other, West Germany.
The wall was built in 1961. Families and friends were suddenly split apart. Many could not visit each other for years.
The two sides lived very differently. The West was free and rich; the East was ruled by a strict government with much less freedom.
People in the East wanted change. In 1989, huge but peaceful crowds marched in the streets.
On November 9, 1989, the government finally opened the gates. Crowds climbed the wall, hugged, and cried with joy.
People broke the wall apart with hammers. That night changed Germany — and the world — forever.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A wall that divided Berlin and the night it came down
How to build a strong wall
Why the wall was built in 1961
q.why: 全文講分隔柏林的圍牆，以及它倒下的那一夜。

q.q: When was the Berlin Wall built?
q.why: 第二段：The wall was built in 1961。

q.q: What happened on November 9, 1989?
opts: Soldiers knocked the whole wall down that night
The government opened the gates and crowds climbed the wall
q.why: 第五段：the government finally opened the gates…Crowds climbed the wall。

q.q: In the text, “split apart” means ___.
q.why: split apart = 被拆散、分開；家人與朋友被圍牆分隔兩邊。

q.q: Why did the crowds “cry with joy”?
opts: They could finally be free and reach loved ones again
q.why: 圍牆開放代表自由、能再與親友相見，所以喜極而泣。

gt.en: For 28 years, a long concrete wall cut the city of Berlin in two.
gt.zh: 二十八年來，一道長長的水泥牆把柏林這座城市切成兩半。

gt.en: The wall was built in 1961.
gt.zh: 這道牆建於 1961 年。

gt.en: The West was free and rich; the East was ruled by a strict government with much less freedom.
gt.zh: 西邊自由又富裕；東邊則由嚴格的政府統治，自由少得多。

gt.en: In 1989, huge but peaceful crowds marched in the streets.
gt.zh: 1989 年，龐大但和平的群眾在街上遊行。

b.title: A Wall, and the People Who Ended It
text: For nearly three decades, the Berlin Wall was the world's most famous symbol of division. Built in 1961, it sealed off communist East Germany from the free, democratic West, cutting straight through the heart of Berlin.
The wall was more than concrete. Guards, fences, and watchtowers stopped East Germans from fleeing west, and some who tried were killed. Families were separated for a generation.
By 1989, pressure was building across Eastern Europe. Reforms in the Soviet Union and brave, peaceful protests in East German cities made the old rulers look weak.
Then, on the evening of November 9, 1989, a confused government announcement suggested the border was open. Thousands rushed to the crossings, and the overwhelmed guards simply raised the barriers.
What followed was pure celebration. Strangers embraced, people danced on top of the wall, and crowds began to chip it away with hammers and chisels.
Less than a year later, East and West Germany were reunited. The fall of the wall came to stand for the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The Berlin Wall divided Germany for decades, and its peaceful fall in 1989 ended the Cold War in Europe.
The wall was good for Berlin.
A confused announcement led guards to open the border in 1989.
q.why: 核心：圍牆分裂德國數十年，1989 年和平倒下，象徵歐洲冷戰結束。

q.q: What did the wall separate?
opts: Communist East Germany from the democratic West
q.why: 第一段：sealed off communist East Germany from the free, democratic West。

q.q: Why did the guards raise the barriers on November 9?
opts: The leaders had planned to open the border that night
A confused announcement suggested the border was open, and crowds overwhelmed them
q.why: 第四段：混亂的宣布讓人以為邊界開放，人潮湧來、警衛招架不住就抬起了柵欄。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “fleeing” means ___.
q.why: flee = 逃離；圍牆阻止東德人逃往西方。

q.q: What did the fall of the wall come to symbolize?
opts: The start of the Cold War
The peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe
q.why: 末段：came to stand for the peaceful end of the Cold War in Europe。

tr.en: For nearly three decades, the Berlin Wall was the world's most famous symbol of division.
tr.zh: 將近三十年來，柏林圍牆是全世界最有名的分裂象徵。

tr.en: Reforms in the Soviet Union and brave, peaceful protests in East German cities made the old rulers look weak.
tr.zh: 蘇聯的改革，加上東德各城市勇敢而和平的抗議，讓舊的統治者顯得軟弱。

tr.en: Thousands rushed to the crossings, and the overwhelmed guards simply raised the barriers.
tr.zh: 成千上萬的人衝向檢查哨，不知所措的守衛乾脆把柵欄升了起來。

c.title: The Night History Turned
text: Some walls are built to keep enemies out; the Berlin Wall was built to keep a population in. For twenty-eight years it stood as the Cold War made concrete — a 155-kilometre scar dividing not only a city but two visions of how human beings should live.

Its fall, on the night of 9 November 1989, was almost an accident. A muddled press conference, a misread note, a spokesman's uncertain words — and suddenly East Germans were walking, unhindered, toward checkpoints that had meant death to cross. The guards, awaiting orders that never came, stepped aside.

What makes the night remarkable is less the politics than the restraint. A heavily armed border, decades of resentment, vast crowds — and yet almost no violence. The revolution was carried out with hammers against stone, not against people.
The consequences were immense: Germany reunified within a year, the Soviet bloc dissolved, and the long standoff that had shadowed the twentieth century quietly ended.

Yet the wall also leaves a warning. It was raised in a single night and took a generation to fall — a reminder of how quickly freedom can be enclosed, and how much courage, and patience, it can take to open it again.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central point?
opts: The wall was an engineering triumph.
The guards planned the fall carefully.
The wall's peaceful fall ended an era — and warns how easily freedom can be lost and how hard it is to regain.
The wall fell because the leaders carefully planned to open it.
q.why: 主旨：圍牆和平倒下終結一個時代，也警示自由多麼容易被封閉、重獲又多麼艱難。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “restraint” refers to ___.
opts: holding back from violence despite anger and arms
q.why: restraint = 克制；儘管武裝、積怨、人潮眾多，雙方卻幾乎沒有動用暴力。

q.q: Why does the writer call the fall “almost an accident”?
opts: The leaders decided to open the border, but the date was chosen by chance
A confused announcement and hesitant guards, not a clear decision, opened the border
q.why: 第二段：混亂的記者會、誤讀的字條、猶疑的發言，加上等不到命令的警衛，意外促成了開放。

q.q: What warning does the final paragraph give?
opts: Freedom can be enclosed quickly but takes courage and patience to restore
q.why: 末段：圍牆一夜築起、卻用了一個世代才倒下——提醒自由易失難得。

q.q: How does the essay move from beginning to end?
opts: From a list of dates to a map
From the wall's purpose and fall, to its consequences, to a wider lesson
From a recipe to a review
q.why: 結構：圍牆的目的與倒下 → 後續影響 → 更大的啟示。

discuss: Why do you think the fall of the wall happened with so little violence?
Walls and borders still divide people today. When is a border fair, and when is it not?
The wall rose in a night but took years to fall. What does that tell us about freedom?

topic: Chang'e Flies to the Moon
zh: 嫦娥奔月
src: National Geographic · Taiwan News · The New York Times

a.title: Chang'e Flies to the Moon
text: Long ago in China, there were ten suns in the sky. They burned the land, and the people suffered.
A brave archer named Houyi shot down nine of the suns. He left just one, to give light and warmth.
As a reward, Houyi was given a special medicine. If one person drank it, they would live forever.
Houyi's wife was named Chang'e. One day, to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself.
At once, Chang'e began to float. She rose up and up, all the way to the moon, where she still lives today.
Every Mid-Autumn Festival, people look at the full moon and remember beautiful, lonely Chang'e.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: How Chang'e went to live on the moon
How Houyi shot down nine suns
q.why: 全文是嫦娥奔月、住到月亮上的故事。

q.q: What did the archer Houyi do?
opts: He built a house on the moon
He shot down nine of the ten suns
q.why: 第二段：shot down nine of the suns，留下一個太陽。

q.q: Why did Chang'e drink the medicine?
opts: Houyi asked her to drink it so they could live forever
To keep it safe from a thief
q.why: 第四段：to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself。

q.q: In the story, an “archer” is a person who ___.
q.why: archer = 弓箭手；后羿射下九個太陽。

q.q: Why do people remember Chang'e at the Mid-Autumn Festival?
opts: Because they see the full moon, where she is said to live
q.why: 末段：中秋賞圓月時，人們想起住在月亮上的嫦娥。

gt.en: Long ago in China, there were ten suns in the sky.
gt.zh: 很久以前在中國，天上有十個太陽。

gt.en: A brave archer named Houyi shot down nine of the suns.
gt.zh: 一位名叫后羿的勇敢射手射下了其中九個太陽。

gt.en: As a reward, Houyi was given a special medicine.
gt.zh: 作為獎賞，后羿得到了一種特別的藥。

gt.en: One day, to keep the medicine safe from a thief, she drank it herself.
gt.zh: 有一天，為了不讓藥被小偷拿走，她自己把它喝了下去。

b.title: The Lady in the Moon
text: One of China's best-loved myths explains the shape many people see in the full moon. It begins with a sky scorched by ten suns.
A heroic archer, Houyi, saved the world by shooting down nine of them. For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.
Houyi loved his wife, Chang'e, and did not want to leave her behind, so he hid the elixir at home. But one day, while he was away, a greedy student tried to steal it.
To stop the thief, Chang'e swallowed the elixir herself. She became weightless and drifted up into the sky, finally coming to rest on the cold, silver moon.
There she has lived ever since, the stories say, with only a jade rabbit for company — forever near the world she loved, yet unable to return to it.
Each Mid-Autumn Festival, families gaze at the round moon and think of Chang'e: a tale of love, sacrifice, and the ache of separation.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The moon is made of rabbits.
Houyi was rewarded with an elixir for shooting down the suns.
A myth of love and sacrifice explains how Chang'e came to live, alone, on the moon.
q.why: 核心：這則關於愛與犧牲的神話，解釋嫦娥為何獨自住在月亮上。

q.q: What reward did Houyi receive?
q.why: 第二段：rewarded him with an elixir of immortality。

q.q: What happened after Chang'e swallowed the elixir?
opts: She became weightless and drifted up to the moon
q.why: 第四段：She became weightless and drifted up…to the moon。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “immortality” means ___.
q.why: immortality = 永生、不死。

q.q: What is the main feeling at the heart of the story?
opts: Love and sacrifice, and the sadness of separation
q.why: 末段：a tale of love, sacrifice, and the ache of separation。

tr.en: It begins with a sky scorched by ten suns.
tr.zh: 故事從一片被十個太陽烤焦的天空開始。

tr.en: For this, the gods rewarded him with an elixir of immortality — enough for one person to live forever.
tr.zh: 為此，眾神賞給他一瓶長生不老藥——剛好夠一個人永遠活下去。

tr.en: Houyi loved his wife, Chang'e, and did not want to leave her behind, so he hid the elixir at home.
tr.zh: 后羿深愛他的妻子嫦娥，不想丟下她，所以他把仙藥藏在家裡。

c.title: What We See in the Moon
text: Every culture that has gazed at the moon has told stories to explain its marks. In China, those marks are Chang'e — a goddess whose legend turns a bright object in the sky into an image of longing.

The tale is deceptively simple. Her husband, the archer Houyi, wins an elixir of immortality; to keep it from a thief, Chang'e drinks it herself and floats, irreversibly, to the moon. What begins as a rescue ends as an exile.

The myth's power lies in its ambivalence. Chang'e gains eternal life but loses everything that made life worth living — her home, her husband, the warm and ordinary world below. Immortality, the story quietly suggests, can be its own kind of prison.

That is perhaps why the legend binds itself so naturally to the Mid-Autumn Festival, a celebration of reunion. Families gathered beneath the full moon are reminded, by the lonely figure within it, of exactly what they have — and how precious togetherness is.
