A myth, in the end, is a mirror held up to a people's values. In Chang'e, China sees not only a goddess, but a meditation on sacrifice, distance, and the bittersweet cost of living forever.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The moon is cold and silver.
Houyi should have drunk the elixir.
Chang'e's myth turns the moon into an image of longing and a meditation on sacrifice and the cost of immortality.
Chang'e's myth shows that living forever is the greatest reward.
q.why: 主旨：嫦娥神話把月亮化為思念的意象，省思犧牲與「永生的代價」。

q.q: In paragraph 2, the writer says the story “ends as an exile,” meaning Chang'e is ___.
opts: forced to live far away, unable to return
q.why: exile = 流放；她永遠離開、無法返回人間。

q.q: What does “immortality…can be its own kind of prison” suggest?
opts: Living forever may cost you everything that made life meaningful
The elixir did not really make her immortal
q.why: 第三段：嫦娥得永生，卻失去家、丈夫與人間——永生反而像一座牢。

q.q: Why does the legend pair so naturally with a festival of reunion?
opts: Because her loneliness reminds gathered families how precious togetherness is
q.why: 第四段：月中孤影讓團圓的家庭更珍惜「在一起」。

q.q: The final paragraph frames a myth as ___.
opts: a mirror of a people's values
q.why: 末段：神話是映照一個民族價值觀的鏡子。

discuss: Would you want to live forever if it meant leaving everyone you love? Why or why not?
Many cultures see shapes or stories in the moon. Why do you think humans do this?
Chang'e's story is tied to a festival about reunion. What makes being together precious to you?

topic: World Food Day
zh: 世界糧食日

a.title: Food for Everyone
text: October 16 is World Food Day. It is a day to think about food and the people who do not have enough of it.
Food gives us energy to live, learn, and play. But not everyone has enough to eat.
Around the world, hundreds of millions of people go to bed hungry. Many of them are children.
At the same time, a lot of food is wasted. People and shops throw away food that is still good to eat.
We can all help. Take only what you will eat. Save your leftovers. Share food with people in need.
When we grow, share, and respect food, we can build a world where no one is hungry.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Food, hunger, and not wasting food
Why World Food Day is on October 16
q.why: 全文談食物、飢餓，以及不要浪費食物。

q.q: When is World Food Day?
q.why: 第一段：October 16 is World Food Day。

q.q: What does the text say happens to a lot of food?
opts: It is wasted or thrown away
It is given to hungry people
q.why: 第四段：a lot of food is wasted…throw away food that is still good to eat。

q.q: In the text, “leftovers” are ___.
opts: food not eaten that you keep for later
q.why: leftovers = 剩菜、吃剩留著之後吃的食物。

q.q: How can YOU help, according to the text?
opts: Buy food you will not eat
Take only what you will eat and share with others
q.why: 第五段：Take only what you will eat. Save your leftovers. Share food with people in need。

gt.en: It is a day to think about food and the people who do not have enough of it.
gt.zh: 這是一個思考食物、以及那些吃不飽的人的日子。

gt.en: Food gives us energy to live, learn, and play.
gt.zh: 食物給我們生活、學習和玩耍的能量。

gt.en: Around the world, hundreds of millions of people go to bed hungry.
gt.zh: 全世界有好幾億人餓著肚子上床睡覺。

gt.en: At the same time, a lot of food is wasted.
gt.zh: 同時，卻有很多食物被浪費掉。

b.title: Enough for All?
text: Every year on 16 October, the United Nations marks World Food Day, led by its Food and Agriculture Organization, or FAO. The date asks an uncomfortable question: why, on a planet that grows plenty, do so many still go hungry?
The numbers are stark. Hundreds of millions of people do not get enough to eat, and hunger has risen in recent years because of conflict, drought, and high prices.
Waste makes the problem worse. Studies suggest that roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away — spoiled on farms, damaged in transport, or scraped off plates in wealthy homes.

The causes are tangled, but solutions exist. Farmers can grow crops that survive a changing climate, shops and families can waste less, and fairer systems can help food reach the people who need it most.
Food is also about health and culture. A good meal is not only fuel; it brings families together and carries the taste of home.
The message of World Food Day is both practical and hopeful: there is enough for everyone, if only we grow, share, and value it wisely.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: The world does not grow enough food, so many people go hungry.
The world grows plenty, yet many go hungry — through waste and unfair access — and this can change.
q.why: 核心弔詭：地球生產足夠糧食，卻仍有許多人挨餓，原因在浪費與分配不公，而這是可以改變的。

q.q: Which organization leads World Food Day?
opts: The FAO, part of the United Nations
q.why: 第一段：led by its Food and Agriculture Organization, or FAO。

q.q: About how much food is lost or wasted?
q.why: 第三段：roughly a third of all food produced is lost or thrown away。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “spoiled” means the food ___.
opts: went bad and became unsafe to eat
q.why: spoil = （食物）腐壞、變質。

q.q: What is the main paradox the text points to?
opts: The world produces enough food, yet many are still hungry
q.why: 第一段的核心矛盾：a planet that grows plenty，卻仍有許多人挨餓。

tr.en: A good meal is not only fuel; it brings families together and carries the taste of home.
tr.zh: 一頓好飯不只是燃料；它讓家人團聚，也承載著家的味道。

c.title: The Paradox of the Full Plate
text: Each 16 October the United Nations observes World Food Day, an occasion built around a paradox: humanity grows more than enough food to feed itself, and yet hundreds of millions remain hungry.

The contradiction deepens on closer look. Even as some go without, roughly a third of all food produced is never eaten — lost to poor storage in poorer countries, and to sheer waste in richer ones. The world, in effect, starves and squanders at the same time.

Hunger is rarely a simple shortage of food; more often it is a failure of access. War drives families from their fields, drought ruins harvests, and inflation puts the market stall beyond reach. Where food is treated purely as a commodity, those with the least money eat last.

None of this is beyond human repair. Hardier crops, better storage, shorter supply chains, and policies that treat food as a right rather than a privilege could, together, narrow the gap. So could a cultural shift away from waste in kitchens and supermarkets alike.
World Food Day, at its best, refuses an easy despair. It insists that hunger in an age of plenty is not a natural disaster but a human choice — and therefore one that humans can unmake.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Hunger amid plenty is a human choice — caused by waste and unequal access — and so it can be changed.
Hunger exists mainly because the world cannot grow enough food.
The world should grow less food.
q.why: 末段點題：豐足時代的飢餓不是天災，而是人為選擇，因此人也能終結它。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “squander” means to ___.
q.why: squander = 揮霍、浪費。starves and squanders 形成「一邊挨餓、一邊浪費」的對照。

q.q: “Hunger…is a failure of access” suggests that the main problem is ___.
opts: there is simply not enough food in the world
people cannot reach or afford the food that exists
farmers need to grow much more food
q.why: 第三段：飢餓多半不是總量不足，而是「取得」出了問題——戰爭、乾旱、通膨讓人買不到、拿不到。

q.q: The phrase “refuses an easy despair” shows the writer is ___.
opts: concerned but ultimately hopeful that change is possible
q.why: 作者拒絕輕易的絕望，強調飢餓可以被人類「解開」，語氣憂心卻抱持希望。

q.q: What does paragraph 2 (“The contradiction deepens”) mainly do?
opts: Develop the paradox by showing waste alongside hunger
q.why: 第二段延伸第一段的弔詭：一邊有人挨餓，一邊卻有三分之一的食物被浪費。

discuss: How much food does your family throw away? How could you waste less?
Is having enough food a basic right? Whose job is it to make sure everyone can eat?
Food brings people together. What dish means “home” to you, and why?

topic: Rome: The Eternal City
zh: 羅馬：永恆之城
src: The New York Times · National Geographic · BBC

a.title: Welcome to Rome
text: Rome is the capital city of Italy. People call it the 'Eternal City' because it is so very old.
Almost two thousand years ago, Rome ruled a huge empire. You can still see many things the Romans built.
The Colosseum is a giant stone stadium. Long ago, thousands of people watched games and shows there.
At the Trevi Fountain, visitors throw a coin over their shoulder and make a wish to return one day.
Rome is also famous for its food — pizza, pasta, and creamy gelato ice cream.
Old and new live side by side. You might drink coffee next to a building that is two thousand years old.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Rome, a very old city, and what to see there
q.why: 全文介紹古老的羅馬與值得一看的景點。

q.q: Why is Rome called the 'Eternal City'?
opts: Because it is so very old
Because it was built by the gods
q.why: 第一段：the 'Eternal City' because it is so very old。

q.q: What do visitors do at the Trevi Fountain?
opts: Throw a coin and make a wish to return
q.why: 第四段：throw a coin over their shoulder and make a wish to return。

q.q: In the text, an “empire” is ___.
opts: a large group of lands ruled by one power
q.why: empire = 帝國；古羅馬曾統治廣大的帝國。

q.q: What does “old and new live side by side” mean?
opts: Ancient and modern things exist together in the same city
q.why: 末段：在兩千年的老建築旁喝咖啡——古今並存。

gt.en: Rome is the capital city of Italy.
gt.zh: 羅馬是義大利的首都。

gt.en: Almost two thousand years ago, Rome ruled a huge empire.
gt.zh: 將近兩千年前，羅馬統治著一個龐大的帝國。

gt.en: The Colosseum is a giant stone stadium.
gt.zh: 羅馬競技場是一座巨大的石造競技場。

b.title: The Eternal City
text: Rome, the capital of Italy, has been called the 'Eternal City' for two thousand years — and it wears its age proudly.
At its height, ancient Rome ruled much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. The remains of that empire still fill the modern streets.
The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument. Nearby lie the ruins of the Forum, the beating heart of the ancient city.
Rome is also layered with art and faith. Within it sits the Vatican, home of the Pope, where visitors line up to see Michelangelo's painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel.
Yet Rome is no museum. Scooters weave through narrow lanes, markets spill across old squares, and families argue happily over plates of pasta.
To walk through Rome is to walk through time itself — from a Roman temple, to a Renaissance church, to a modern café, often within a single street.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Rome is mainly a quiet museum of the ancient world.
Only the Pope lives in Rome.
Rome blends an ancient empire with living, modern life, so visiting it is like walking through time.
q.why: 核心：羅馬把古帝國與現代生活交疊，遊覽其中彷彿穿越時空。

q.q: How many spectators could the Colosseum hold?
q.why: 第三段：once held fifty thousand spectators。

q.q: What can visitors see at the Vatican?
opts: Michelangelo's ceiling in the Sistine Chapel
q.why: 第四段：Michelangelo's painted ceiling in the Sistine Chapel。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “spectators” are ___.
q.why: spectator = 觀眾；競技場曾容納五萬名觀眾。

q.q: What does “Rome is no museum” suggest?
opts: The Vatican museums are closed to visitors
Rome is not just a quiet display of the past; it is full of busy, everyday life
q.why: 第五段：機車穿梭、市集熱鬧、家人為義大利麵熱烈討論——羅馬是活生生的城市。

tr.en: Rome, the capital of Italy, has been called the 'Eternal City' for two thousand years — and it wears its age proudly.
tr.zh: 義大利的首都羅馬被稱為「永恆之城」已經兩千年了——而它也驕傲地展現自己的年紀。

tr.en: The remains of that empire still fill the modern streets.
tr.zh: 那個帝國的遺跡至今仍遍布現代的街道。

tr.en: The Colosseum, a vast arena that once held fifty thousand spectators, remains the city's most famous monument.
tr.zh: 曾經能容納五萬名觀眾的巨大競技場——羅馬競技場，至今仍是這座城市最有名的古蹟。

c.title: A City Built on Itself
text: No city carries its past quite like Rome. Three thousand years of history are not neatly preserved here but piled up, layer upon layer, so that an ancient temple may support a medieval church that now shades a modern bus stop.

The scale of the old city still astonishes. The Colosseum, where crowds once roared at gladiators, and the Pantheon, whose vast dome has stood unbroken for nearly nineteen centuries, remind visitors that the Romans built not merely for their own age but, it seems, for all of them.
Layered atop the empire is another Rome — the spiritual capital of the Catholic world, its skyline crowned by the dome of St Peter's, its galleries holding some of the greatest art ever made.
To live among such grandeur is a daily negotiation. Romans complain, fairly, of crowds, traffic, and the burden of maintaining a city that belongs, in a sense, to the whole world.
And yet the city endures, as it always has — not by freezing its past, but by living inside it, turning ruins into backdrops and history into the ordinary scenery of everyday life.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's central idea?
opts: Rome should be turned into a museum.
Rome survives by living inside its layered past, making history part of everyday life.
Rome has lost all its history.
Rome's ancient buildings matter more than its modern life.
q.why: 主旨：羅馬不是把過去封存，而是「活在其中」，讓歷史成為日常的一部分。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “astonishes” means ___.
q.why: astonish = 使驚嘆；古城的規模令訪客驚嘆。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying the Romans built “for all ages”?
opts: They built only for the emperors of their own time
They only built for one year
Their works were so lasting they still stand and serve today
q.why: 第二段：萬神殿圓頂近十九世紀屹立不倒——羅馬人彷彿為所有世代而建。

q.q: What does paragraph 4 add to the picture?
opts: Living among such heritage is also a daily burden of crowds, traffic, and upkeep
q.why: 第四段坦承：與偉大遺產共生也是日常的負擔——人潮、交通與維護。

q.q: The essay is mainly built around the image of ___.
opts: layers — history piled up and lived in
q.why: 全文以「層層交疊、活在其中」的意象貫穿。

discuss: Rome mixes 2,000-year-old ruins with daily life. Would you enjoy living somewhere like that? Why?
Protecting old monuments costs a lot. Who should pay to protect world heritage — the city, the country, or the world?
Throwing a coin in the Trevi Fountain is a wish to return. What wish-customs do you know from Taiwan or elsewhere?

topic: Icarus and the Fall
zh: 伊卡洛斯的墜落
src: National Geographic · BBC Culture · The New York Times

a.title: The Boy Who Flew Too High
text: Long ago, in an old Greek story, a clever man named Daedalus and his son Icarus were trapped on an island.
To escape, Daedalus made two big pairs of wings. He joined feathers together with soft wax.
Before they flew, Daedalus warned his son. “Do not fly too low, or the sea will wet your wings. Do not fly too high, or the sun will melt the wax.”
At first, Icarus was careful. But flying felt wonderful, and soon he forgot his father's words.
He flew higher and higher, close to the sun. The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and Icarus dropped into the sea.
People still tell this story today. It teaches us to be brave — but also to listen, and to know our limits.

q.q: What is this story mainly about?
opts: A boy who flew too high and fell
How Daedalus made wings from feathers and wax
q.why: 全文是伊卡洛斯飛得太高、最後墜落的故事。

q.q: How did Daedalus make the wings?
q.why: 第二段：feathers together with soft wax。

q.q: What did the father warn Icarus NOT to do?
opts: Not to fly too high, because the sun would melt the wax — but flying low was safe
Not to fly too high (near the sun) or too low (near the sea)
q.why: 第三段：別飛太低（海會弄濕翅膀），也別飛太高（太陽會融化蠟）。

q.q: In the story, “melt” means to ___.
opts: turn soft or liquid from heat
q.why: melt = 融化；太陽的熱把蠟融化了。

q.q: What lesson does the story teach?
opts: Be brave, but also listen and know your limits
The sun is close to the sea
q.why: 末段：be brave — but also to listen, and to know our limits。

gt.en: To escape, Daedalus made two big pairs of wings.
gt.zh: 為了逃走，代達洛斯做了兩對大翅膀。

gt.en: Before they flew, Daedalus warned his son.
gt.zh: 在他們飛走之前，代達洛斯警告了他的兒子。

gt.en: The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and Icarus dropped into the sea.
gt.zh: 蠟融化了，他的翅膀散開，伊卡洛斯掉進了海裡。

gt.en: He joined feathers together with soft wax.
gt.zh: 他用軟蠟把羽毛黏在一起。

b.title: Between the Sea and the Sun
text: One of the most famous of all Greek myths tells of Daedalus, a brilliant inventor, and his son Icarus, imprisoned on the island of Crete by King Minos.
Daedalus devised a daring escape. From feathers and wax he built two great pairs of wings, so that he and his son might simply fly away.
He gave Icarus one firm warning: fly a middle course. Too low, and the sea's spray would weigh the feathers down; too high, and the sun's heat would melt the wax.
For a while the plan worked, and the two rose into the open sky. But Icarus, thrilled by the sheer power of flight, ignored his father and soared ever upward toward the sun.
The wax softened, the feathers loosened, and the boy plunged into the sea that still bears his name. Daedalus flew on alone, grief-stricken.
For thousands of years the tale has been read as a warning against pride and recklessness — yet some also see in Icarus the beauty of daring to reach for something far greater than yourself.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Daedalus warned Icarus not to fly too high or too low.
Icarus ignored a warning, flew too high, and fell — a story read as both a caution and an act of daring.
q.why: 核心：伊卡洛斯不聽勸、飛太高而墜落；此故事既是警世，也被視為一種勇於追求的壯舉。

q.q: Who imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus, and where?
opts: King Minos, on the island of Crete
q.why: 第一段：imprisoned on the island of Crete by King Minos。

q.q: What were the two dangers in the warning?
opts: Flying too low (sea spray) and too high (the sun's heat)
q.why: 第三段：太低會被海浪弄濕，太高會被太陽融化蠟。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “soared” means ___.
q.why: soar = 翱翔、高飛；伊卡洛斯不斷往上朝太陽飛去。

q.q: Why does the last paragraph offer two readings of the story?
opts: Because one reading is true and the other is a mistake
Because the myth can mean both “don't be reckless” and “it is beautiful to dare greatly”
q.why: 末段並陳兩種解讀：對傲慢魯莽的警告，以及勇於追求更高目標的美好。

tr.en: From feathers and wax he built two great pairs of wings, so that he and his son might simply fly away.
tr.zh: 他用羽毛和蠟做了兩對大翅膀，好讓他和兒子可以直接飛走。

tr.en: He gave Icarus one firm warning: fly a middle course.
tr.zh: 他給了伊卡洛斯一個嚴厲的警告：要在中間的高度飛。

tr.en: But Icarus, thrilled by the sheer power of flight, ignored his father and soared ever upward toward the sun.
tr.zh: 但是伊卡洛斯被飛翔的力量沖昏了頭，不理會父親的話，一直往上朝著太陽高飛。

c.title: The Two Lessons of Icarus
text: Few images from mythology have proved as enduring as the fall of Icarus: a boy, feathered wings melting, dropping from a bright sky into an indifferent sea. For nearly three thousand years the Greek tale has been retold, painted, and argued over — chiefly because it refuses to mean only one thing.

The conventional reading is a caution against hubris. Warned by his father Daedalus to keep a middle course, Icarus flew too close to the sun, and his pride — or his carelessness — destroyed him. In this version the moral is restraint: know your limits, and heed those wiser than you.

Yet a second reading has grown louder in modern times. Icarus, after all, did what humankind had only dreamed of — he flew. If his reach exceeded his grasp, perhaps the reaching itself was glorious, and a life spent hugging the safe middle is its own kind of failure.

Tellingly, the myth gives us both a reckless son and a cautious father, and it is the son we remember. Daedalus survives, yet it is Icarus whose name endures — as if the story cannot quite decide whether to mourn his fall or admire his flight.
That unresolved tension is the myth's genius. It hands each listener a mirror and asks a question as old as ambition itself: how high is too high?

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The myth's only lesson is that pride always leads to a fall.
The myth endures because it holds two opposing lessons — a warning against pride and a tribute to daring — and refuses to choose.
q.why: 全文主旨：此神話之所以不朽，正因它同時容納「警戒傲慢」與「歌頌勇敢」兩種對立解讀，且不作取捨。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “hubris” means ___.
q.why: hubris = 傲慢、過度自信，是傳統解讀中伊卡洛斯墜落的原因。

q.q: Why does the writer note that it is Icarus, not Daedalus, whom we remember?
opts: Because the story is quietly drawn to the daring son as much as to the careful father
Because Icarus was the one who built the wings
q.why: 第四段：謹慎的父親活下來，但後世記得的是勇敢的兒子——暗示故事對「敢飛」的傾慕不亞於對謹慎的肯定。

q.q: What is the writer's stance on which lesson is correct?
opts: Firmly on the side of caution
q.why: 作者刻意不下定論，以「how high is too high?」收尾，保留開放。

q.q: How is the essay structured?
opts: As two contrasting readings of the same myth, then a reflection on their tension
As a timeline of Greek history
As a travel guide to Crete
q.why: 第2段傳統解讀、第3段現代解讀，第4–5段再反思兩者的張力——對比結構。

discuss: Which lesson do you take from Icarus — be careful, or be bold? Why?
Have you ever ignored good advice and learned something the hard way?
Is it better to aim very high and risk failing, or to choose a safe, steady path?

topic: La Tomatina: The Great Tomato Fight
zh: 番茄節：西班牙丟番茄大戰

a.title: The Great Tomato Fight
text: In a small town in Spain called Buñol, there is one very messy festival. It is called La Tomatina.
On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square. They all want to throw tomatoes!
Big trucks bring in piles of soft, ripe tomatoes — more than one hundred tons of them.
When the signal is given, everyone throws tomatoes at each other for one hour. Soon the whole street is red!
The rule is simple: squash each tomato first, so it is soft and does not hurt anyone.
After the fight, fire trucks spray the streets clean. Everyone is covered in tomato, laughing and happy.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A messy Spanish festival where people throw tomatoes
How fire trucks clean the streets after a festival
q.why: 全文介紹西班牙丟番茄的狂歡節慶 La Tomatina。

q.q: When does La Tomatina happen?
q.why: 第二段：On the last Wednesday of August。

q.q: What is the main rule?
opts: Squash each tomato first so it does not hurt anyone
Throw as hard as you can
Throw the tomatoes for as long as you want
q.why: 第五段：squash each tomato first, so it is soft and does not hurt anyone。

q.q: In the text, “ripe” means a tomato that is ___.
opts: fully grown and soft, ready to eat
q.why: ripe = 成熟的；成熟的番茄才軟。

q.q: Why do fire trucks spray the streets afterwards?
opts: To wash away the tomato mess and clean the streets
q.why: 丟完番茄滿地紅漿，消防車噴水清洗街道。

gt.en: In a small town in Spain called Buñol, there is one very messy festival.
gt.zh: 在西班牙一個叫做布尼奧爾的小鎮，有一個非常髒亂的節慶。

gt.en: On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people meet in the town square.
gt.zh: 在八月的最後一個星期三，成千上萬的人聚集在鎮上的廣場。

gt.en: Big trucks bring in piles of soft, ripe tomatoes — more than one hundred tons of them.
gt.zh: 大卡車運來一堆堆又軟又熟的番茄——總共超過一百噸。

gt.en: When the signal is given, everyone throws tomatoes at each other for one hour.
gt.zh: 信號一響，大家就互相丟番茄，丟整整一個小時。

b.title: A Town Painted Red
text: Once a year, the quiet Spanish town of Buñol, near Valencia, turns bright red. On the last Wednesday of August, it hosts La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight.
Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets — far more than the town's own population. Trucks arrive loaded with over a hundred tons of ripe tomatoes.
At a signal, the battle begins. For one glorious, chaotic hour, strangers hurl tomatoes at anyone within reach, until the streets run with red pulp.
There are a few rules. Tomatoes must be squashed before they are thrown, so they cannot injure anyone, and the fight stops the moment a second signal sounds.
No one is quite sure how it began — perhaps a street scuffle among young people in 1945 — but the tradition stuck, and today it draws visitors from all over the world.
Afterwards, the townspeople hose down the streets, and the tomato juice leaves the old stones unusually clean. The mess, it turns out, washes away easily — and the memories last.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: La Tomatina is the world's biggest food fight, a wild one-hour tradition that draws visitors worldwide.
About 20,000 people throw tomatoes in Buñol each year.
q.why: 核心：La Tomatina 是全球最大的食物大戰，一小時的瘋狂傳統吸引各國遊客。

q.q: How many people join, roughly?
q.why: 第二段：Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets。

q.q: What are two of the rules?
opts: Squash tomatoes first; stop at the second signal
Pay to throw; bring your own
Bring a ladder; count to ten
q.why: 第四段：先壓扁番茄，第二次信號響起就停止。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “hurl” means to ___.
q.why: hurl = 用力投擲。

q.q: What does the text say about how the festival began?
opts: No one is quite sure, but it may have grown from a 1945 street scuffle
It was started in 1945 by the town's leaders as a planned event
A company invented it last year
q.why: 第五段：起源不明，可能源於 1945 年的街頭衝突，後來成了傳統。

tr.en: On the last Wednesday of August, it hosts La Tomatina, the world's biggest food fight.
tr.zh: 在八月的最後一個星期三，這裡會舉辦番茄節——全世界規模最大的食物大戰。

tr.en: Around twenty thousand people pack the narrow streets — far more than the town's own population.
tr.zh: 大約兩萬人擠滿狹窄的街道——遠遠超過這個小鎮本身的人口。

tr.en: For one glorious, chaotic hour, strangers hurl tomatoes at anyone within reach, until the streets run with red pulp.
tr.zh: 在這精彩又混亂的一小時裡，陌生人把番茄用力丟向身邊的任何人，直到街上流滿紅色的果肉。

c.title: The Serious Business of Play
text: To an outsider, La Tomatina looks like pure chaos: twenty thousand people, a hundred tons of tomatoes, and one hour of cheerful violence in the streets of a small Spanish town. Yet beneath the mess lies something worth taking seriously — the human need to play.

The festival's origins are humble and uncertain, probably a spontaneous squabble among young people in 1945 that was simply repeated the next year, and the next, until accident hardened into tradition.

What endures is not meaning but release. In everyday life we are told to be careful, clean, and controlled; for one hour, La Tomatina suspends all of that, inviting ordinary adults to be gleefully ridiculous with the full permission of their town.
There is even a quiet logic to the tomato. Soft, cheap, and harmless once squashed, it allows a kind of combat with no real victims — aggression turned entirely into joy.

Every culture builds such safety valves, from carnivals to festivals of colour. La Tomatina is simply one of the loudest: proof that a community sometimes needs, together, to make a glorious and meaningless mess — and then wash it clean.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Beneath the chaos, La Tomatina answers a real human need — to play, let go, and release pressure together.
The festival has a deep ancient meaning that most visitors miss.
Food fights are dangerous and should stop.
q.why: 主旨：混亂底下，La Tomatina 回應了人類「一起玩樂、釋放壓力」的真實需求。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “spontaneous” means ___.
q.why: spontaneous = 自發、臨時起意的；一場即興的爭吵演變成傳統。

q.q: Why does the writer say the tomato has “a quiet logic”?
opts: Soft and harmless once squashed, it allows combat that turns aggression into joy, with no real victims
Tomatoes are cheap, so the town can buy many
q.why: 第四段：壓扁後柔軟無害的番茄，讓「戰鬥」沒有真正的受害者，把攻擊性全化為歡樂。

q.q: How does the writer treat this messy festival?
opts: As playful on the surface but genuinely meaningful underneath
q.why: 作者把表面的胡鬧看作有深意——「認真看待玩樂」。

q.q: What idea ties the whole essay together?
opts: That societies need 'safety valves' where people can let go together
q.why: 全文以「社會需要安全閥、讓人一起釋放」的概念貫穿。

discuss: Why do you think people enjoy festivals that are messy or a little wild?
La Tomatina lets ordinary adults be 'ridiculous' for an hour. Why might that be healthy?
What festivals in Taiwan or elsewhere act as a 'safety valve' for people to let go?

topic: International Sloth Day
zh: 國際樹懶日：慢慢來的生存高手

a.title: The Slowest Animal in the Trees
text: October 20 is International Sloth Day. It is a day to learn about one of the slowest animals in the world.
Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America. They spend almost all their life high up in the trees.
A sloth moves very slowly. It hangs upside down from branches with its long, curved claws.
Sloths eat leaves. Leaves do not give much energy, so sloths save energy by moving slowly and sleeping a lot.
Their fur is often a little green. Tiny plants called algae grow in it! This helps sloths hide in the trees.
Today, many forests are cut down. Sloth Day reminds people to protect the forests where sloths live.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Sloths and why they live slowly
How to keep a sloth as a pet
How sloths hide in the trees with green fur
q.why: 全文介紹樹懶的生活方式，以及國際樹懶日的意義。

q.q: Where do sloths live?
opts: In the rainforests of Central and South America
q.why: 第二段：Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America。

q.q: Why do sloths move slowly?
opts: Leaves give little energy, so they save energy
They are lazy and do not like to move
q.why: 第四段：Leaves do not give much energy, so sloths save energy by moving slowly。

q.q: In the text, “claws” are ___.
opts: the long, sharp nails on an animal's feet
q.why: claws = 爪子；樹懶用彎彎的長爪子掛在樹枝上。

q.q: Why is green fur useful for a sloth?
opts: It keeps the sloth warm in snow
It helps the sloth swim faster
It helps the sloth hide among the leaves
It makes the sloth taste bad
q.why: 第五段：綠色的藻類讓樹懶在樹上更不容易被發現（This helps sloths hide in the trees）。

gt.en: Sloths live in the rainforests of Central and South America.
gt.zh: 樹懶住在中美洲和南美洲的雨林裡。

gt.en: It hangs upside down from branches with its long, curved claws.
gt.zh: 牠用又長又彎的爪子倒掛在樹枝上。

gt.en: Leaves do not give much energy, so sloths save energy by moving slowly and sleeping a lot.
gt.zh: 樹葉提供的能量不多，所以樹懶靠著慢慢移動和多睡覺來節省能量。

gt.en: Tiny plants called algae grow in it!
gt.zh: 有一種叫做藻類的微小植物長在牠的毛裡！

b.title: Slow and Steady Survives
text: Every October 20, wildlife groups celebrate International Sloth Day, a date created in Colombia in 2010 to raise awareness about one of the rainforest's most unusual animals.
Sloths live in the treetops of Central and South America. There are two main groups, two-toed and three-toed sloths, and both spend nearly their whole lives hanging upside down from branches.

Their famous slowness is not laziness but a clever survival strategy. Sloths live on a diet of leaves, which contain very little energy, so their bodies run at an extremely low speed — they even digest food slowly, sometimes over several days.
Moving slowly also keeps them safe. Eagles and big cats notice movement, and a sloth that barely moves is hard to spot, especially since algae growing in its fur gives it a greenish colour.
Surprisingly, sloths are good swimmers, and they climb down to the ground only about once a week — mainly to go to the toilet.
Their biggest dangers today come from people: forests cleared for farms and roads, electric power lines, and illegal trading of babies as pets.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Sloths are lazy animals that should move more.
Sloths come down to the ground only about once a week.
International Sloth Day started in Africa.
A sloth's slowness is a smart way to survive, but people now threaten its forests.
q.why: 核心：慢是聰明的生存策略，但現在人類的開發威脅牠們。

q.q: Where and when did International Sloth Day begin?
q.why: 第一段：a date created in Colombia in 2010。

q.q: How often do sloths usually come down to the ground?
q.why: 第五段：only about once a week — mainly to go to the toilet。

q.q: In paragraph 4, “spot” means to ___.
q.why: spot 在這裡是動詞：發現、看見。幾乎不動的樹懶很難被發現。

q.q: Why does moving slowly protect a sloth from eagles?
opts: Predators notice movement, so a still sloth is hard to see
Eagles cannot see the colour green
q.why: 第四段：Eagles and big cats notice movement——不動就不容易被發現。

tr.en: Sloths live in the treetops of Central and South America.
tr.zh: 樹懶住在中美洲和南美洲的樹頂上。

tr.en: Their famous slowness is not laziness but a clever survival strategy.
tr.zh: 牠們出了名的慢並不是懶惰，而是一種聰明的生存策略。

tr.en: Their biggest dangers today come from people: forests cleared for farms and roads, electric power lines, and illegal trading of babies as pets.
tr.zh: 如今牠們最大的危險來自人類：為了開闢農田和道路而砍伐的森林、電線，以及把幼獸當寵物非法買賣。

c.title: The Wisdom of Slowness
text: In a culture that prizes speed, the sloth is an easy joke: the patron saint of laziness, a creature that seems to have opted out of effort altogether. International Sloth Day, held every October 20, invites us to look again.

A sloth's pace is not a flaw but an exquisitely tuned economy. Its diet of tough, low-calorie leaves would starve a more ambitious animal, so the sloth simply spends less — a slow metabolism, little muscle, and a body temperature that drifts with the air around it.
Even its stillness is strategic. Harpy eagles and jaguars hunt by detecting motion; an animal that barely moves, its fur tinted green by algae, all but disappears into the canopy.

Yet the very trait that has served sloths for millions of years leaves them helpless against modern threats. They cannot outrun a bulldozer, and as roads and power lines cut through the forest, an animal designed for patience meets a world that has run out of it.

Perhaps that is the day's quiet lesson. Success need not mean doing more, faster; sometimes it means fitting your life precisely to what your surroundings can give — and asking whether we are leaving room for creatures who live by a different clock.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: Sloths are lazy and will soon disappear.
The sloth is slow because its body is badly designed.
International Sloth Day should be cancelled.
The sloth's slowness is a finely tuned survival design — one that now struggles in a fast, human-changed world.
q.why: 主旨：慢是精巧的生存設計，但在被人類加速改變的世界裡反而吃虧。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “metabolism” refers to ___.
opts: how fast the body uses energy
q.why: metabolism = 新陳代謝；樹懶代謝慢，所以耗能少。

q.q: Why does the writer call the sloth's pace “an exquisitely tuned economy”?
opts: Its slow body carefully matches the very little energy its diet provides
Sloths trade leaves with other animals
Sloths are worth a lot of money
Sloths save energy by sleeping most of the day
q.why: 第二段：低熱量的樹葉只能支撐「省著用」的身體——像精打細算的經濟。

q.q: How does the writer view the common joke that sloths are lazy?
q.why: 開頭先提「懶惰」的刻板印象，再邀請讀者 look again——作者認為這是誤解。

q.q: How is the essay organised?
opts: A list of sloth species and their sizes
It challenges a stereotype, explains the science, notes modern threats, then draws a wider lesson
A story about one sloth's life
A comparison of sloths and jaguars
q.why: 結構：挑戰刻板印象 → 說明科學 → 現代威脅 → 引申人生啟示。

discuss: Sloths survive by doing less, not more. Can you think of a time when going slowly was the smarter choice?
Which human activities in the text put sloths in danger? What could people change?
If an animal is famous for being 'lazy', does that change how people care about protecting it?

topic: Alfred Nobel: The Man Behind the Prize
zh: 諾貝爾：獎項背後的那個人
src: Nobel Prize Outreach · TIME · The Economist

a.title: The Man Who Started the Nobel Prize
text: Every year, the world talks about the Nobel Prize. But who was Nobel? His name was Alfred Nobel. He was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on October 21, 1833.
Alfred loved science and languages. When he grew up, he became an inventor.
His most famous invention was dynamite. It was very strong and helped workers build roads, tunnels and railways.
But dynamite was also used in wars. This made Alfred sad. He wanted people to remember him for something good.
So he wrote a special plan: after his death, his money would give prizes to people who help the world.
Today the Nobel Prize goes to great scientists, writers and peacemakers every year.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How dynamite helped build roads and railways
The life of Alfred Nobel and why he created the Nobel Prize
q.why: 全文介紹諾貝爾的生平，以及他為什麼設立諾貝爾獎。

q.q: When and where was Alfred Nobel born?
q.why: 第一段：born in Stockholm, Sweden, on October 21, 1833。

q.q: How did dynamite help workers?
opts: It helped them build roads, tunnels and railways
q.why: 第三段：helped workers build roads, tunnels and railways。

q.q: In the text, an “inventor” is a person who ___.
opts: makes something new for the first time
q.why: inventor = 發明家，創造出新東西的人。

q.q: Why did Alfred Nobel create the prizes?
opts: He wanted to be remembered for something good
He wanted more people to buy dynamite
Because dynamite made him very rich
He wanted to win a prize himself
q.why: 第四段：He wanted people to remember him for something good。

gt.en: Every year, the world talks about the Nobel Prize.
gt.zh: 每年，全世界都在談論諾貝爾獎。

gt.en: When he grew up, he became an inventor.
gt.zh: 他長大以後，成為了一位發明家。

gt.en: His most famous invention was dynamite.
gt.zh: 他最有名的發明是炸藥。

gt.en: But dynamite was also used in wars.
gt.zh: 但是炸藥也被用在戰爭中。

b.title: From Dynamite to the Nobel Prize
text: Each October the world waits for the Nobel Prize announcements. October 21 is the birthday of the man behind them: Alfred Nobel, born in Stockholm in 1833.
Nobel grew up partly in Russia, spoke several languages and became a gifted chemist. Over his life he collected 355 patents, but one invention made his fortune: dynamite, patented in 1867.

Dynamite made the dangerous liquid nitroglycerin much safer to handle, and it transformed the building of mines, tunnels and railways. Yet it was also used in weapons, and Nobel himself owned factories that made arms.

In 1888, when his brother Ludvig died, a French newspaper reportedly mixed up the brothers and printed Alfred's obituary instead, calling him a 'merchant of death'. Historians are not sure how much this shocked him, but the story is often told.

In 1895, in Paris, Nobel signed a will that left most of his huge fortune to fund prizes for those who had brought 'the greatest benefit to humankind' in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.
He died in Italy on December 10, 1896. The first prizes were awarded in 1901, and they are still presented on December 10 every year.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Dynamite was the safest invention ever.
Nobel collected 355 patents during his life.
The Nobel Prize is only for scientists.
Alfred Nobel, the inventor of dynamite, used his fortune to create prizes that reward benefits to humankind.
q.why: 核心：發明炸藥致富的諾貝爾，用財富設立獎勵造福人類者的獎項。

q.q: How many patents did Nobel collect?
q.why: 第二段：he collected 355 patents。

q.q: Why are the prizes presented on December 10?
opts: It is the day Nobel died
It is the day dynamite was invented
It is the day Nobel signed his will
q.why: 最後一段：He died … on December 10, 1896 … presented on December 10 every year。

q.q: In paragraph 4, an “obituary” is ___.
opts: a newspaper report about someone who has died
q.why: obituary = 訃聞，報紙上報導某人過世的文章。

q.q: Why does the writer say the 'merchant of death' story is “reportedly” true and “often told”?
opts: Because historians are not completely sure of the details
q.why: 第四段：Historians are not sure——作者用 reportedly 表示這是流傳的說法，未必完全可靠。

tr.en: Each October the world waits for the Nobel Prize announcements.
tr.zh: 每年十月，全世界都在等待諾貝爾獎的公布。

tr.en: Over his life he collected 355 patents, but one invention made his fortune: dynamite, patented in 1867.
tr.zh: 他一生擁有 355 項專利，但讓他致富的是一項發明：1867 年取得專利的炸藥。

tr.en: Dynamite made the dangerous liquid nitroglycerin much safer to handle, and it transformed the building of mines, tunnels and railways.
tr.zh: 炸藥讓危險的液體硝化甘油變得安全許多、更好處理，也徹底改變了礦坑、隧道和鐵路的建造方式。

c.title: A Fortune in Search of a Conscience
text: Few names are as firmly attached to virtue as Nobel's — which is a curious fate for a man who made his fortune from explosives. Born in Stockholm on October 21, 1833, Alfred Nobel was a restless polyglot chemist whose 355 patents included the one that defined him: dynamite.

His invention tamed nitroglycerin, a liquid so unstable that it had killed workers, including Nobel's own younger brother in an 1864 factory blast. Packed into a safer form, it blasted open mines, canals and railways across the industrial world — and, inevitably, found its way into war.

Legend holds that in 1888 a French newspaper, mistaking his brother Ludvig's death for his own, branded him 'the merchant of death'. The anecdote is almost too neat, and historians treat it with caution; still, it captures a real tension in a man who wrote poetry, never married, and seemed uneasy with the source of his wealth.

Whatever his motives, his will of 1895 was radical. It bypassed his relatives and directed most of his estate towards prizes, regardless of nationality, for those who had conferred 'the greatest benefit to humankind'.

More than a century later, the prizes are less a monument to Nobel than a standing argument about what benefit means — and a reminder that how a fortune is spent can, in the end, redefine how it was made.

q.q: Which best captures the essay's central idea?
opts: Nobel created the prizes because a newspaper called him a 'merchant of death'.
The prizes have nothing to do with Nobel.
A man who grew rich from explosives used his will to tie his name to the benefit of humankind, reshaping how his fortune is remembered.
q.why: 主旨：靠炸藥致富的人，以遺囑把名字和「造福人類」綁在一起，改寫了財富的意義。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “unstable” describes nitroglycerin as ___.
opts: likely to explode or change suddenly
q.why: unstable = 不穩定；硝化甘油容易突然爆炸。

q.q: Why does the writer call the 'merchant of death' story “almost too neat”?
opts: Because it was printed in a tidy newspaper
Because it fits the story so perfectly that it may have been simplified or exaggerated
Because historians have proved the story is completely false
q.why: 第三段：故事完美得「太剛好」，所以史學家持保留態度。

q.q: What is the writer's attitude towards Nobel's motives?
opts: Open and careful — the motives are uncertain, but the will mattered
q.why: Whatever his motives…——作者不下定論，但肯定遺囑的影響。

q.q: How does the final paragraph relate to the opening?
opts: It repeats the list of patents
It returns to the irony of virtue and explosives, concluding that spending a fortune can redefine its origins
q.why: 首尾呼應：開頭的反差（美德 vs. 炸藥）在結尾以「怎麼花錢可以改寫錢的來歷」收束。

discuss: Nobel's invention helped build railways but was also used in wars. Can one invention be both good and bad?
If you could create a prize for people who help the world, what would it reward?
Do you think how people spend their money can change how others remember them?

topic: Machu Picchu: The Lost City of the Inca
zh: 馬丘比丘：印加的天空之城
src: UNESCO · National Geographic · The New York Times

a.title: A City in the Clouds
text: High in the mountains of Peru, there is an old stone city. Its name is Machu Picchu.
The Inca people built it more than 500 years ago. It sits on top of a mountain, about 2,400 metres high. Clouds often float around it.
The Inca were great builders. They cut big stones so well that the stones fit together without any cement.
There are houses, temples and long steps on the mountain called terraces. People grew food on them.
Today, many visitors come to see Machu Picchu. Some walk for four days on an old path called the Inca Trail.
Only a certain number of visitors can enter each day. This helps protect the old city.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How the Inca grew food on terraces
An old Inca city on a mountain in Peru
q.why: 全文介紹秘魯山上的印加古城馬丘比丘。

q.q: How high is Machu Picchu?
q.why: 第二段：about 2,400 metres high。

q.q: What did the Inca grow food on?
opts: Big stones fitted together without cement
q.why: 第四段：long steps … called terraces. People grew food on them。

q.q: In the text, “cement” is something used to ___.
q.why: cement = 水泥，用來黏合石塊；印加人不用水泥就能讓石頭密合。

q.q: Why can only a certain number of visitors enter each day?
opts: To protect the old city from damage
The city is too small for anyone
q.why: 最後一段：This helps protect the old city——控制人數以保護古蹟。

gt.en: It sits on top of a mountain, about 2,400 metres high.
gt.zh: 它位在一座大約兩千四百公尺高的山頂上。

gt.en: They cut big stones so well that the stones fit together without any cement.
gt.zh: 他們把大石頭切得非常好，石頭不用任何水泥就能緊密地拼在一起。

gt.en: There are houses, temples and long steps on the mountain called terraces.
gt.zh: 山上有房子、神廟，還有一層層叫做梯田的長階梯。

gt.en: Today, many visitors come to see Machu Picchu.
gt.zh: 今天，許多遊客來參觀馬丘比丘。

b.title: Peru's Citadel Above the Clouds
text: Perched on a narrow ridge in the Andes, about 2,430 metres above sea level, Machu Picchu is one of the most breathtaking places on Earth.
The Inca built it in the mid-1400s, probably as a royal estate for the emperor Pachacuti. Less than a century later the site was abandoned, around the time the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire.

Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact. Local farmers always knew it was there, but it became world-famous after the American explorer Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.
Its stonework is remarkable. Builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, and the walls have survived centuries of earthquakes.
In 1983 the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today visitors arrive by train and bus from Cusco, or hike the famous Inca Trail, which usually takes four days.
Popularity brings problems, however. To prevent damage, Peru limits daily visitor numbers and sets fixed routes through the ruins.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Machu Picchu was built by the Spanish.
Machu Picchu is a modern hotel.
Machu Picchu, a remarkably preserved Inca site high in the Andes, is now a protected world treasure.
Hiram Bingham made Machu Picchu famous in 1911.
q.why: 核心：保存完好的印加遺址，如今是受保護的世界遺產。

q.q: Why did Machu Picchu survive largely intact?
opts: It was rebuilt by the Spanish after they found it
q.why: 第三段：Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact。

q.q: What do the builders' walls NOT use?
q.why: 第四段：fit together without mortar。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “abandoned” means ___.
q.why: abandoned = 被遺棄、廢棄。

q.q: What does the writer suggest by saying “Local farmers always knew it was there”?
opts: Bingham did not really 'discover' it; he made it famous to the outside world
The farmers hid it from Bingham
q.why: 第三段：當地人一直知道它的存在，賓漢只是讓它聞名國際（publicised）。

tr.en: Less than a century later the site was abandoned, around the time the Spanish conquered the Inca Empire.
tr.zh: 不到一百年後，這個地方就被遺棄了，大約就在西班牙人征服印加帝國的時候。

tr.en: Because the Spanish never found it, Machu Picchu survived largely intact.
tr.zh: 因為西班牙人從來沒有找到它，馬丘比丘大致完整地保存了下來。

tr.en: Builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar, and the walls have survived centuries of earthquakes.
tr.zh: 建造者把花崗岩塊切得非常精準，不用灰泥就能拼合，這些牆經歷了好幾個世紀的地震依然屹立。

c.title: The City That Was Never Lost
text: Machu Picchu is routinely called a 'lost city', a phrase that says more about the outside world than about the place itself. Set on a saddle of rock some 2,430 metres up in the Peruvian Andes, it was never truly lost to the people who farmed the slopes below.

Built in the mid-fifteenth century, most likely as an estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, it was occupied for less than a hundred years. When the Spanish conquest shattered the empire, the site simply fell quiet — and, crucially, it escaped the colonisers' attention, sparing it the destruction suffered by so many Inca temples.

What survives is an argument in stone. Granite blocks were shaped to fit so closely that no mortar was needed, and the slightly flexible joints have let the walls ride out earthquakes that toppled later buildings.

Hiram Bingham's 1911 expedition turned the site into an international icon, but it also reflected an era in which foreign 'discovery' erased local knowledge, and artefacts he removed were returned to Peru only in this century.

Today the danger is love rather than neglect. With crowds pressing on fragile terraces, Peru caps daily entries and fixes routes — a reminder that a place can survive centuries of isolation and still be worn away by admiration.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall argument?
opts: Machu Picchu was lost for centuries until Bingham discovered it.
Machu Picchu was never really 'lost'; its story reveals outside perspectives, and today its greatest threat is too much attention.
Tourists should not care about history.
q.why: 主旨：「失落之城」反映的是外界視角；今天最大的威脅反而是過多的喜愛。

q.q: In paragraph 5, “fragile” means ___.
q.why: fragile = 脆弱、容易損壞的；梯田承受不了大量人潮。

q.q: Why does the writer say the phrase 'lost city' “says more about the outside world”?
opts: Because only outsiders lost track of it — locals always knew it was there
Because outsiders get lost on the trail
Because the city was hidden so well that even local people had forgotten it
q.why: 第一段：當地農民一直知道它，「失落」是外界的說法。

q.q: How does the writer present Bingham's 'discovery'?
opts: With a critical eye — it made the site famous but erased local knowledge
q.why: 第四段：既讓它成為國際象徵，也反映了抹去在地知識的時代——帶批判的平衡觀點。

q.q: What contrast frames the final paragraph?
opts: Centuries of isolation versus damage caused by admiration
q.why: 最後一段：撐過幾世紀的孤立，卻可能被「愛」磨損——danger is love rather than neglect。

discuss: Why do you think the Inca built a city on top of a mountain?
Is it fair to say an explorer 'discovered' a place that local people already knew? Why or why not?
Famous places can be damaged by too many visitors. What rules would you make to protect a site like this?

topic: Mole Day: Counting the Tiny
zh: 莫耳日：怎麼數數不清的原子？

a.title: A Day for a Very Big Number
text: October 23 is Mole Day. It is not about the little animal! It is a day for chemistry.
Everything is made of atoms. Atoms are so small that we cannot see them, even with a normal microscope.
Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups. One group is called a mole.
One mole is about 602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 things. People write it as 6.02 × 10²³.
That is why Mole Day is on 10/23, from 6:02 in the morning to 6:02 in the evening.
On Mole Day, students do fun experiments, bake cakes and make puns about moles.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: A small animal that digs holes
Why 6.02 is an important number in maths
Mole Day, a day about counting atoms in chemistry
q.why: 全文介紹化學界的莫耳日與「莫耳」這個計數單位。

q.q: Why do scientists count atoms in big groups?
opts: Atoms are too heavy to weigh one by one
Atoms are tiny, so there are too many to count one by one
q.why: 第三段：Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups。

q.q: When does Mole Day start?
opts: At 6:02 in the morning on October 23
q.why: 第五段：on 10/23, from 6:02 in the morning。

q.q: In the text, “tiny” means ___.
q.why: tiny = 極小的。

q.q: Why is Mole Day on 10/23?
opts: It is the birthday of the animal
It is the start of winter

gt.en: It is a day for chemistry.
gt.zh: 這是一個屬於化學的日子。

gt.en: Everything is made of atoms.
gt.zh: 所有的東西都是由原子組成的。

gt.en: Because atoms are tiny, scientists count them in big groups.
gt.zh: 因為原子非常微小，科學家就把它們一大群一大群地計算。

gt.en: On Mole Day, students do fun experiments, bake cakes and make puns about moles.
gt.zh: 在莫耳日，學生們做有趣的實驗、烤蛋糕，還會說關於莫耳（鼴鼠）的雙關笑話。

b.title: Why Chemists Celebrate at 6:02
text: Every year on October 23, chemistry classrooms celebrate Mole Day. The party runs from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m., and the timing is a clue to what it honours.
In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles. Just as a 'dozen' means twelve, a mole means about 6.02 × 10²³ — a six followed by twenty-three digits.
This value is known as Avogadro's number, named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, whose ideas in the early 1800s helped explain how gases behave.
Why such an enormous number? Atoms are unimaginably small. A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
Using moles lets chemists connect the invisible world of atoms to amounts they can actually weigh on a scale, which is essential for medicine, cooking chemistry and industry.
Mole Day began in American schools in the 1980s, and today teachers mark it with experiments, mole-shaped cakes and plenty of terrible puns.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Mole Day celebrates the mole, a huge counting unit that links tiny atoms to amounts we can weigh.
Moles are animals that live underground.
Amedeo Avogadro was an Italian scientist.
Water is made of one atom.
q.why: 核心：莫耳日慶祝「莫耳」這個巨大的計數單位，它把原子世界和可秤量的份量連起來。

q.q: Who is Avogadro's number named after?
q.why: 第三段：named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro。

q.q: About how much water contains one mole of water molecules?
q.why: 第四段：A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole。

q.q: In paragraph 2, a “unit” is ___.
opts: a standard amount used for measuring or counting
q.why: unit = 單位，例如 dozen 是「打」，mole 是「莫耳」。

q.q: Why does the writer compare a mole to a 'dozen'?
opts: Because a mole and a dozen are the same number
To show both are ways of counting things in groups
q.why: 第二段：Just as a 'dozen' means twelve——用熟悉的「一打」說明莫耳也是成組計數。

tr.en: Every year on October 23, chemistry classrooms celebrate Mole Day.
tr.zh: 每年十月二十三日，化學教室都會慶祝莫耳日。

tr.en: In chemistry, a mole is not an animal but a unit for counting particles.
tr.zh: 在化學裡，莫耳不是一種動物，而是計算粒子的單位。

tr.en: A single sip of water — about 18 grams — contains roughly one mole of water molecules.
tr.zh: 一小口水——大約十八公克——就含有大約一莫耳的水分子。

c.title: A Bridge Between Two Worlds
text: On October 23, from 6:02 in the morning until 6:02 at night, chemistry teachers indulge in a ritual of cakes, costumes and shameless puns. Mole Day is silly by design, but the number it celebrates is one of the quiet pillars of modern science.

A mole is simply a counting unit — like a dozen, only vastly larger. It stands for roughly 6.02 × 10²³ particles, a quantity named in honour of Amedeo Avogadro, the Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules.

Avogadro's idea was largely ignored in his lifetime. Only decades after his death did chemists recognise how neatly it untangled the confusion over atomic weights, and the constant bearing his name was measured with real precision only much later.

The mole's genius lies in translation. Atoms are far too small to count or weigh individually, yet a mole of any substance has a mass in grams that matches its atomic or molecular weight. A sip of water, about eighteen grams, contains a mole of water molecules — a number larger than the grains of sand on many beaches combined.
Mole Day, then, celebrates a bridge: between the invisible and the measurable, and between an overlooked idea and its eventual vindication.

q.q: Which best captures the essay's main idea?
opts: Avogadro's idea was ignored during his lifetime.
Behind a playful holiday lies the mole, a key idea that connects the invisible world of atoms to what we can measure.
q.why: 主旨：輕鬆節日背後，是連接原子世界與可測量世界的關鍵概念。

q.q: In the last paragraph, “vindication” means ___.
opts: proof that an idea was right after all
q.why: vindication = 被證明正確；亞佛加厥的想法最終獲得平反。

q.q: What does paragraph 3 suggest about how science sometimes works?
opts: Good ideas are always accepted at once
A correct idea can be ignored for years before others recognise its value
Famous scientists' ideas are accepted quickly
q.why: 第三段：他的想法生前被忽視，死後數十年才被認可。

q.q: How does the writer view the silliness of Mole Day?
opts: As a waste of class time
As playful on the surface but celebrating something genuinely important
q.why: silly by design, but … one of the quiet pillars——表面胡鬧，實則重要。

q.q: What image ties the essay together?
opts: The mole as a 'bridge' between the invisible and the measurable
q.why: 結尾的 bridge 意象收束全文——連接看不見與可測量的世界。

discuss: Why do you think scientists need special units like the mole to talk about atoms?
Avogadro's idea was ignored for years. Can you think of other ideas that were laughed at before people accepted them?
Should school subjects have 'fun days' like Mole Day? Which subject would you choose, and how would you celebrate?

topic: World Polio Day
zh: 世界小兒麻痺日：只差最後一步

a.title: Almost Gone for Good
text: October 24 is World Polio Day. Polio is a disease caused by a virus. It mostly makes young children sick.
Polio can hurt the body's nerves. Some children cannot walk again after they get it.
In the past, polio was common all over the world. Parents were very afraid of it.
Then scientists made vaccines. One was a shot, and later one was a few drops in the mouth. The drops are cheap and easy to give.
Since then, millions of children have got the vaccine. Polio is now almost gone. Taiwan has been free of polio for many years.
But the virus is still found in a few places. World Polio Day reminds us to finish the job.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: Why polio still exists in a few places
Polio, a disease that vaccines have almost ended
q.why: 全文介紹小兒麻痺，以及疫苗如何讓它幾乎消失。

q.q: Who does polio mostly make sick?
q.why: 第一段：It mostly makes young children sick。

q.q: Why are the vaccine drops useful?
opts: They work after only one drop for life
They are cheap and easy to give
q.why: 第四段：The drops are cheap and easy to give。

q.q: In the text, “common” means ___.
q.why: common = 常見的；過去小兒麻痺在世界各地都很常見。

q.q: What does “finish the job” mean in the last sentence?
q.why: 病毒還在少數地方，「完成工作」指讓小兒麻痺在全世界徹底消失。

gt.en: Polio is a disease caused by a virus.
gt.zh: 小兒麻痺是一種由病毒引起的疾病。

gt.en: Polio can hurt the body's nerves.
gt.zh: 小兒麻痺會傷害身體的神經。

gt.en: In the past, polio was common all over the world.
gt.zh: 過去，小兒麻痺在世界各地都很常見。

gt.en: But the virus is still found in a few places.
gt.zh: 但是在少數幾個地方，仍然可以找到這種病毒。

b.title: The Last Mile Against Polio
text: Every October 24, health workers mark World Polio Day, an awareness day started by Rotary International to honour the fight against one of history's most feared childhood diseases.
Polio is caused by a virus that spreads mainly through contaminated water and hands. In a small number of cases it attacks the nerves and can cause lifelong paralysis.

In the early 1950s, epidemics left thousands of children unable to walk each year. In 1955 a vaccine developed by a team led by Jonas Salk was declared safe and effective, and a few years later Albert Sabin's oral vaccine — given as drops — made mass vaccination cheap and simple.

In 1988 the World Health Organization and its partners launched a global campaign to end polio. Back then, the disease paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year. Since then, cases have fallen by more than 99 percent.
Wild poliovirus now survives in only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan, where conflict and distrust make it hard to reach every child.
Taiwan was certified polio-free as part of its region in 2000. Experts warn, though, that as long as the virus exists anywhere, every country must keep vaccinating.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Wild poliovirus survives only in Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Vaccines have nearly wiped out polio, but the final cases are the hardest, so vaccination must continue.
q.why: 核心：疫苗讓小兒麻痺幾乎絕跡，但最後一哩最難，接種不能停。

q.q: How much have polio cases fallen since 1988?
q.why: 第四段：cases have fallen by more than 99 percent。

q.q: Where does wild poliovirus still survive?
q.why: 第五段：only two countries, Pakistan and Afghanistan。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “contaminated” water is water that is ___.
q.why: contaminated = 受汙染的，帶有病菌。

q.q: Why must polio-free countries keep vaccinating?
opts: Because polio is still common in most countries
Because the virus could travel back from places where it still exists
Because the law has no end date
q.why: 最後一段：as long as the virus exists anywhere——病毒仍可能被帶回來。

tr.en: Polio is caused by a virus that spreads mainly through contaminated water and hands.
tr.zh: 小兒麻痺是由一種病毒引起的，主要透過受汙染的水和手傳播。

tr.en: In the early 1950s, epidemics left thousands of children unable to walk each year.
tr.zh: 在 1950 年代初期，每年的疫情都讓好幾千名孩子無法走路。

tr.en: In 1988 the World Health Organization and its partners launched a global campaign to end polio.
tr.zh: 1988 年，世界衛生組織和它的夥伴發起了一場終結小兒麻痺的全球行動。

c.title: Why the Last One Percent Is the Hardest
text: There are few public-health stories as triumphant, or as unfinished, as polio's. World Polio Day, marked each October 24, celebrates a disease driven to the brink of extinction — and admits how stubbornly it clings on.

In the first half of the twentieth century, summer polio epidemics emptied swimming pools and terrified parents; the virus, usually silent, occasionally invaded the nervous system and left children paralysed. The 1955 announcement that Jonas Salk's injected vaccine worked was greeted almost like the end of a war, and Albert Sabin's oral drops later made immunisation affordable on a mass scale.

When the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988, polio paralysed an estimated 350,000 children a year in more than 125 countries. Cases have since fallen by over 99 percent, and wild virus persists in just two, Pakistan and Afghanistan.

Yet the final fraction is the most expensive and the most fragile. The remaining cases sit where conflict blocks vaccinators, where rumours breed suspicion, and where a single missed child can seed a new outbreak.

Eradication, after all, is unforgiving arithmetic: ninety-nine percent is not a near-success but an unfinished task. Only smallpox has ever been fully defeated in humans; polio's last mile will test whether the world can sustain attention long after a crisis stops feeling urgent.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's argument?
opts: Polio is almost gone, but the last tiny fraction is the hardest to end and demands lasting effort.
Polio cases have fallen by more than 99 percent, so the work is done.
q.why: 主旨：幾乎消滅，但最後一小部分最難，需要持續投入。

q.q: In the final paragraph, “eradication” means ___.
q.why: eradication = 根除、徹底消滅。

q.q: Why does the writer call eradication “unforgiving arithmetic”?
opts: Because doctors must be good at maths
Because anything short of 100 percent still leaves the job unfinished
Because the last cases are cheap and easy to stop
q.why: 99% 不算接近成功，而是「尚未完成」——只要有殘留，病毒就可能再起。

q.q: How would you describe the writer's tone?
q.why: 既肯定 triumphant 的成果，也強調 unfinished——讚揚中帶警惕。

q.q: How is the essay structured?
opts: A comparison of two countries' food
Past fear → vaccine breakthroughs → global progress → why the last cases are hardest → a wider challenge
q.why: 結構：昔日恐懼 → 疫苗突破 → 全球進展 → 最後一哩的難處 → 更大的挑戰。

discuss: Why do you think the last few cases of a disease are often the hardest to stop?
Polio vaccines changed millions of lives. What other inventions have protected children's health?
If a disease is almost gone, should people keep getting vaccinated? Explain your view.

topic: United Nations Day
zh: 聯合國日
src: The New York Times · The Economist · United Nations

a.title: One Day for the World
text: October 24 is United Nations Day. It celebrates the day the United Nations, or UN, began in 1945.
The UN started after the Second World War. Countries were tired of fighting and wanted to keep peace.
Today, almost every country in the world is a member. They meet and talk instead of fighting.
The UN does many things. It helps people after disasters, sends food and medicine, and protects children's rights.
It also works on big problems that no country can solve alone, like disease, war, and climate change.
United Nations Day reminds us of one simple idea: when countries work together, the world is safer for everyone.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The United Nations and why countries work together
q.why: 全文介紹聯合國，以及各國合作的重要。

q.q: When is United Nations Day?
q.why: 第一段：October 24 is United Nations Day。

q.q: Why did the UN start?
opts: After the Second World War, to keep peace
To stop the Second World War while it was happening
q.why: 第二段：The UN started after the Second World War…wanted to keep peace。

q.q: In the text, a “member” is ___.
opts: a country that belongs to the group
q.why: member = 成員；此處指加入聯合國的國家。

q.q: What is the main lesson of the day?
opts: When countries work together, the world is safer
q.why: 末段：when countries work together, the world is safer for everyone。

gt.en: It celebrates the day the United Nations, or UN, began in 1945.
gt.zh: 它慶祝的是聯合國在 1945 年成立的那一天。

gt.en: Countries were tired of fighting and wanted to keep peace.
gt.zh: 各國厭倦了戰爭，想要維持和平。

gt.en: Today, almost every country in the world is a member.
gt.zh: 今天，世界上幾乎每個國家都是會員。

gt.en: It helps people after disasters, sends food and medicine, and protects children's rights.
gt.zh: 它在災難後幫助人們、送去食物和藥品，並保護兒童的權利。

b.title: When Nations Talk
text: Each year on 24 October, the world marks United Nations Day, the anniversary of the day in 1945 when the UN officially came into being.
The organisation was born from the ruins of the Second World War. Its founders, having seen two world wars in thirty years, hoped that a place where countries could talk might stop a third.
Today the UN has 193 member states — nearly every nation on Earth. They gather in New York to debate, to vote, and, when they can, to agree.
The UN's work reaches far beyond politics. Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.
It is far from perfect. Powerful countries can block decisions, and the UN often cannot force anyone to obey. Critics say it is too slow and too weak.
Yet its defenders point to a simple fact: since 1945 there has been no third world war. Imperfect as it is, a place where enemies must at least talk may be worth keeping.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: New York is the best city on Earth.
The UN, though imperfect, gives nations a place to talk and cooperate instead of fighting.
Only rich countries join the UN.
q.why: 全文重點：聯合國雖不完美，卻提供各國對話與合作、取代戰爭的場所。

q.q: How many member states does the UN have, according to the text?
q.why: 第三段：the UN has 193 member states。

q.q: Which is part of the UN's work beyond politics?
q.why: 第四段：Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children…

q.q: In paragraph 4, a “refugee” is a person who ___.
opts: has been forced to flee their home or country
q.why: refugee = 難民，因戰爭或災難被迫逃離家園的人。

q.q: What is the defenders' main argument in the last paragraph?
opts: Since 1945 there has been no third world war, so a place to talk is worth keeping
The UN makes lots of money
The UN has ended all wars since 1945
q.why: 末段：自 1945 年來未再有第三次世界大戰，說明一個讓敵對雙方至少能對話的地方值得保留。

tr.en: Its founders, having seen two world wars in thirty years, hoped that a place where countries could talk might stop a third.
tr.zh: 它的創立者在三十年內見證了兩次世界大戰，希望一個讓各國可以對話的地方，能阻止第三次世界大戰。

tr.en: They gather in New York to debate, to vote, and, when they can, to agree.
tr.zh: 他們聚集在紐約辯論、投票，並在可能的時候達成共識。

tr.en: Its agencies feed refugees, fight diseases, care for children, protect human rights, and coordinate action on climate change.
tr.zh: 它的各個機構提供難民食物、對抗疾病、照顧兒童、保護人權，並協調對抗氣候變遷的行動。

c.title: An Imperfect Necessity
text: On 24 October the world observes United Nations Day, commemorating the moment in 1945 when a charter signed in San Francisco brought the organisation formally to life.

The UN was an act of exhausted hope. Its architects, surveying a planet twice shattered by world war within a single generation, built not a world government but something humbler: a permanent table around which states, however hostile, would be obliged to sit.

Judged against its loftiest ideals, the UN disappoints. Its Security Council can be paralysed by a single veto; its resolutions are often ignored; its peacekeepers arrive late, or not at all. To its critics it is a mere talking shop, long on words and short on power.

Judged more modestly, the record looks different. UN agencies vaccinate children, shelter refugees, monitor elections, and feed tens of millions; its very existence has made war between great powers, if not impossible, at least harder to begin. Absence, not presence, is often the truer measure of such an institution.
That may be the paradox worth marking each October: an organisation too weak to command and too useful to abandon — an imperfect necessity in a world that has, so far, invented nothing better.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's overall point?
opts: The UN is flawed but remains a useful, hard-to-replace institution for peace.
The UN should be given up.
The UN is flawed, so it should be replaced by something new.
q.why: 末段點題：聯合國是「不完美卻必要」的存在——太弱無法發號施令，卻太有用而不能捨棄。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “however hostile” describes states that are ___.
opts: unfriendly or opposed to each other
q.why: hostile = 敵對的；無論多麼敵對的國家，都必須坐上同一張談判桌。

q.q: What does “Absence, not presence, is often the truer measure” suggest?
opts: The UN is most useful when countries stay away from it
To see the UN's value, imagine a world without it
q.why: 第四段：衡量這類機構的價值，往往要靠想像「若它不存在會如何」，而非只看它在場時的表現。

q.q: How would you describe the writer's attitude toward the UN?
opts: Critical of its weaknesses yet ultimately valuing it
q.why: 作者直言其癱瘓、被忽視等缺點，卻以「imperfect necessity」肯定其價值——批判但終究珍視。

q.q: How are paragraphs 3 and 4 organised?
opts: They tell a story in time order
They contrast a harsh judgement with a more modest defence
q.why: 第3段「以最高理想來評判」（失望），第4段「以較務實標準來看」（成績不同），形成對比結構。

discuss: Should countries always try to solve problems by talking first? When is that hard to do?
The UN is strong in some ways and weak in others. Should it be given more power? Why or why not?
Name one global problem you think only countries working together can solve. How might they start?

topic: Pablo Picasso: Seeing the World in Pieces
zh: 畢卡索：把世界拆開來畫的人
src: Museo Picasso · The Guardian · The New York Times

a.title: The Painter Who Broke the Rules
text: Pablo Picasso was born on October 25, 1881, in Málaga, Spain. He became one of the most famous artists in the world.
Picasso could draw very well when he was a child. His father was an art teacher.
When Picasso was young, he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue. People call this his Blue Period.
Later, he and his friend Georges Braque tried a new way of painting. They showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time. This style is called Cubism.
Picasso made thousands of paintings, drawings and sculptures. He kept working until he was 91 years old.
His art shows us that there is more than one way to see the world.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: The famous artist Picasso and his new ways of painting
Why Picasso painted in blue when he was sad
q.why: 全文介紹畫家畢卡索與他開創的新畫風。

q.q: What was Picasso's father's job?
q.why: 第二段：His father was an art teacher。

q.q: What is Cubism?
opts: Showing faces and objects from many sides at the same time
Painting faces exactly as they look from the front
q.why: 第四段：showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time … called Cubism。

q.q: In the text, a “style” is ___.
opts: a special way of doing something
q.why: style = 風格，做事或創作的獨特方式。

q.q: Why do people call some of his paintings the Blue Period?
opts: He felt sad and painted many pictures in blue
q.why: 第三段：he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue。

gt.en: He became one of the most famous artists in the world.
gt.zh: 他成為了全世界最有名的藝術家之一。

gt.en: When Picasso was young, he felt sad, and he painted many pictures in blue.
gt.zh: 畢卡索年輕的時候很難過，他用藍色畫了許多畫。

gt.en: They showed faces and objects from many sides at the same time.
gt.zh: 他們同時從許多不同的面向來呈現臉孔和物體。

gt.en: Picasso made thousands of paintings, drawings and sculptures.
gt.zh: 畢卡索創作了好幾千件畫作、素描和雕塑。

b.title: The Artist Who Kept Reinventing Himself
text: Born in Málaga, Spain, on October 25, 1881, Pablo Picasso is often called the most influential artist of the twentieth century.
Trained by his father, an art teacher, he showed remarkable skill as a teenager. But he soon grew bored with simply copying what he saw.

In his early twenties he moved between Barcelona and Paris. After the death of a close friend, he painted poor and lonely people in cold shades of blue — the Blue Period — and later turned to warmer pinks and circus performers in his Rose Period.

Around 1907 he painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, a shocking picture of sharp, broken shapes. With his friend Georges Braque he then developed Cubism, a style that shows an object from several viewpoints at once.
In 1937, after German and Italian planes bombed the Spanish town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War, Picasso painted Guernica, a huge black-and-white protest against the horror of war.
He kept experimenting with painting, sculpture and pottery until his death in 1973, leaving behind tens of thousands of works.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: Picasso painted Guernica against the horror of war.
Picasso constantly changed his style and became the most influential artist of his century.
q.why: 核心：畢卡索不斷改變風格，成為二十世紀最具影響力的藝術家。

q.q: What did Picasso paint during his Rose Period?
q.why: 第三段：warmer pinks and circus performers in his Rose Period。

q.q: What was the painting Guernica about?
opts: The horror of war after a town was bombed
q.why: 第五段：a huge black-and-white protest against the horror of war。

q.q: In paragraph 1, “influential” means ___.
opts: having a strong effect on others
q.why: influential = 有影響力的。

q.q: What does the title “Kept Reinventing Himself” suggest?
opts: He invented a new kind of paint
He kept changing his style and trying new ways of making art
q.why: 從藍色時期、玫瑰時期到立體派，他不斷「重新塑造」自己的藝術。

tr.en: Born in Málaga, Spain, on October 25, 1881, Pablo Picasso is often called the most influential artist of the twentieth century.
tr.zh: 1881 年 10 月 25 日出生於西班牙馬拉加的巴勃羅・畢卡索，常被稱為二十世紀最有影響力的藝術家。

tr.en: Trained by his father, an art teacher, he showed remarkable skill as a teenager.
tr.zh: 在當美術老師的父親指導下，他十幾歲時就展現出非凡的才華。

tr.en: With his friend Georges Braque he then developed Cubism, a style that shows an object from several viewpoints at once.
tr.zh: 接著，他和朋友喬治・布拉克發展出立體派，一種同時從好幾個角度呈現物體的風格。

c.title: Why Picasso Painted Faces from Two Sides
text: It is a familiar complaint in galleries: 'My child could paint that.' Pablo Picasso, born in Málaga on October 25, 1881, would hardly have been offended; by his teens he could already draw with academic polish, and he spent the rest of his long life deliberately unlearning it.

His early work was melancholy and lyrical — the cold blues of beggars and outcasts, then the softer roses of acrobats. But around 1907, with Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, he broke with the idea that a painting must imitate a single, fixed view of the world.

Cubism, which he developed alongside Georges Braque, fractured objects into planes and showed them from several angles at once. A face might appear in profile and from the front simultaneously, not because Picasso could not see, but because he wanted to paint what we know about an object, not merely how it looks from one spot.

That restlessness became a method. He moved from painting to collage, sculpture and ceramics, and in Guernica (1937) he turned the bombing of a Basque town into an enduring image of civilian suffering.

Picasso's legacy is complicated, including how he treated the people closest to him. Yet his central provocation endures: that seeing is not a passive act, and that an artist's job may be to show us the world in pieces so that we look at it again.

q.q: Which best captures the writer's main point?
opts: Picasso deliberately broke with realistic painting to show how we know and see things, challenging viewers to look again.
Picasso painted strangely because he never learned to draw realistically.
q.why: 主旨：他刻意拋開寫實，畫出「我們所知道的」物體，挑戰觀眾重新觀看。

q.q: In paragraph 3, “simultaneously” means ___.
q.why: simultaneously = 同時地；一張臉同時呈現側面與正面。

q.q: Why does the writer say Picasso “would hardly have been offended” by 'My child could paint that'?
opts: Because he had mastered realistic drawing early and chose to unlearn it on purpose
q.why: 第一段：他十幾歲就畫得很學院派，之後是刻意「忘掉」這些技巧。

q.q: How does the writer treat Picasso's life and legacy?
opts: With admiration for his art, while acknowledging it is 'complicated'
q.why: 最後一段：legacy is complicated … Yet his central provocation endures——肯定藝術，也承認爭議。

q.q: How does the essay use the opening complaint?
opts: It raises a common misunderstanding that the essay then answers by explaining Picasso's purpose
It starts a story about a child artist
q.why: 以常見質疑開場，再逐步說明畢卡索的用意，回答這個誤解。

discuss: Picasso painted faces from several sides at once. Why might an artist choose not to paint things exactly as they look?
Guernica is a painting against war. Can art change how people feel about a real event?
Should we still admire an artist's work if the artist behaved badly in private life? Explain your view.

topic: The Day Football Got Its Rules
zh: 足球規則誕生的那一天
src: The FA · BBC Sport · The Guardian

a.title: One Game, One Set of Rules
text: Football is the most popular sport in the world. But long ago, there was a big problem: every school played it in a different way.
At some schools, players could carry the ball in their hands. At others, they could kick other players' legs!
On October 26, 1863, a group of men met in London. They started the Football Association, or the FA.
They wrote one set of rules for everyone. Players could not carry the ball, and they could not kick other players.
Some people liked carrying the ball, so they left. Their game later became rugby.
Today, people in almost every country play football with the same rules. It all started at one meeting in London.

q.q: What is this text mainly about?
opts: How football got one set of rules
How rugby became a different game
q.why: 全文介紹 1863 年足球協會成立、統一規則的經過。

q.q: When was the Football Association started?
q.why: 第三段：On October 26, 1863 … They started the Football Association。

q.q: Which rule did the FA make?
opts: Players could carry the ball but not kick other players
Players could not carry the ball
q.why: 第四段：Players could not carry the ball, and they could not kick other players。

q.q: In the text, “popular” means ___.
q.why: popular = 受歡迎的，很多人喜歡。

q.q: Why was having one set of rules important?
opts: So only one school could play
So teams from different places could play the same game together
q.why: 以前各校玩法不同，統一規則後，不同地方的人才能一起比賽。

gt.en: Football is the most popular sport in the world.
gt.zh: 足球是全世界最受歡迎的運動。

gt.en: At some schools, players could carry the ball in their hands.
gt.zh: 在一些學校，球員可以用手拿著球。

gt.en: They started the Football Association, or the FA.
gt.zh: 他們成立了足球協會，也就是 FA。

gt.en: They wrote one set of rules for everyone.
gt.zh: 他們為所有人寫了一套規則。

b.title: How a Pub Meeting Shaped the World's Game
text: On the evening of October 26, 1863, a group of men met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They represented a dozen clubs and schools, and they had one goal: to agree on a single set of rules for football.
At the time, the game was chaotic. Each English school had its own version. Some allowed players to pick up the ball and run; some allowed 'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins.
Led by Ebenezer Morley, a solicitor who had founded his own club, the group formed the Football Association. Over several more meetings they debated what the game should look like.
The biggest arguments were about handling and hacking. When the FA banned both, a few clubs walked out, and their style of play later developed into rugby.
The first Laws of the Game were published in December 1863. Many details have changed since, but the core idea — a kicking game with shared rules — spread around the world.
Even the word 'soccer' comes from the FA: it is a playful short form of 'association football'.

q.q: Which sentence best states the main idea?
opts: An 1863 meeting in London created shared football rules that later spread worldwide.
A few clubs left the FA and started rugby.
q.why: 核心：1863 年倫敦的會議訂出共同規則，之後傳遍全世界。

q.q: What was 'hacking'?
q.why: 第二段：'hacking' — deliberately kicking an opponent's shins。

q.q: What happened when the FA banned handling and hacking?
opts: A few clubs walked out, and their game became rugby
The game was banned in England
q.why: 第四段：a few clubs walked out … later developed into rugby。

q.q: In paragraph 2, “version” means ___.
opts: a different form of the same thing
q.why: version = 版本；每所學校都有自己的足球「版本」。

q.q: Where does the word 'soccer' come from?
q.why: 最後一段：'soccer' … short form of 'association football'。
